e8554b7e24b70680: OCTOBER 16 — Malaysia presents a striking statutory paradox when responding to seasonal haze pollution: the nation possesses a comprehensive, highly punitive domestic environmental legal framework, yet remains entirely powerless against atmospheric smoke originating beyond its borders.

Grounding environmental protection within constitutional jurisprudence is essential, as it establishes an unshakeable bedrock for public rights claims that elevates clean air from a regulatory ideal to a fundamental human right.

The legal foundation for environmental rights in Malaysia originates from Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution, which mandates that no person shall be deprived of their life save in accordance with law.

In the landmark Court of Appeal decision of Tan Tek Seng v Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Pendidikan (1996), the judiciary expansively interpreted the term “life” to encompass all elements that constitute a person’s quality of life.
This precedent has since been established as the legal authority for a constitutional right to live in a reasonably healthy, pollution-free environment.

The practical application of this constitutional principle was demonstrated in 2024 when the Johor Bahru High Court doubled the fine for a company responsible for air pollution in Pasir Gudang to RM80,000 per charge, explicitly citing Article 5 and observing that it guarantees a healthy quality of life.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Motorcyclists ride in the morning in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan on October 14, 2026, amid thick haze from forest and land fires in the region. — AFP pic
That same year, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam) published a dedicated report examining haze pollution through the lens of the right to clean air.

The primary statutory instrument for domestic environmental enforcement is the Environmental Quality Act 1974 (Act 127). Following legislative amendments gazetted on June 6, 2024, and brought into force on July 7, 2024, Parliament amended 28 sections of Act 127, elevating maximum penalties up to RM10 million for severe offences.
To combat atmospheric haze, Section 29A of Act 127 strictly prohibits open burning.
Under the revised penalties, convicted offenders face fines ranging between RM25,000 and RM1 million, imprisonment for terms up to five years, or both.
Furthermore, administrative compounds can now be issued for up to half the maximum statutory fine.
This represents a significant shift from the previous compound baseline of approximately RM2,000, which polluters routinely treated as a mere operational cost cheaper than clearing land by machine.
Section 29A also imposes explicit legal liability on landowners to prevent trespassers from starting fires on their property.
This statutory framework is reinforced by the Environmental Quality (Clean Air) Regulations 2014, which regulate emissions from industrial premises and factories.
In Sarawak — the state most severely impacted by seasonal haze — the Natural Resources and Environment Ordinance 1993 provides the state government with localised environmental regulatory powers.

According to Rosli Zul, Director of the Department of Environment’s Enforcement Division, open burning accounts for nearly 80 per cent of all environmental complaints received annually, prompting intensified enforcement action nationwide.

While these robust domestic environmental statutes establish stringent air quality standards within national borders, public institutions and duty-bearers still face immense administrative and operational hurdles when severe pollution episodes disrupt critical social and economic sectors.
The transboundary jurisdictional deficit and proposals for reform
The fundamental structural flaw in Malaysia’s legal response to haze is territoriality.
Territorial legislation cannot cross international borders to stop transboundary atmospheric pollution, necessitating extra-territorial corporate accountability mechanisms.

The strict territorial limitation of Act 127 allows Malaysian authorities to penalise illegal land clearing in Kuala Langat or Bachok, but leaves them powerless against peat fires burning in Kalimantan, even when those agricultural operations are backed or controlled by Malaysian capital.
The smoke that forced the closure of 710 schools in Sarawak requires no passport to cross international boundaries.
This jurisdictional void has driven recurring calls for a Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
Following the severe 2019 haze crisis, the Academy of Sciences Malaysia was tasked with studying the feasibility of a transboundary pollution legal framework.
The Cabinet approved the introduction of such a bill on February 12, 2020, but the legislative initiative was shelved following a change in government.
In 2023, the government maintained that the option remained under consideration.
By 2024, the incumbent minister argued that enforcing such a law without bilateral agreements posed insurmountable jurisdictional hurdles.
On September 25, the ministry confirmed it had reopened studies into dedicated transboundary legislation, with the minister directing a special committee to conduct an investigation.
Dr G. Pubadi, Undersecretary of the Ministry’s Environmental Management Division, acknowledged that drafting extra-territorial legislation presents complex legal challenges.

To overcome these legal hurdles, future legislation must strategically draw a distinction between extraterritorial in rem land management and in personam regulatory leverage over domestic corporate parents.
Seeking in rem jurisdiction over foreign physical property or foreign sovereign land-use decisions invites legitimate diplomatic resistance regarding state sovereignty.
Conversely, exercising in personam jurisdiction over parent entities registered, listed, or operating within Malaysia is well within established administrative and corporate legal norms.

By embedding mandatory disclosure rules — such as requiring Bursa Malaysia-listed conglomerates to publish detailed maps of foreign agricultural concessions, active fire hotspot data, and foreign subsidiary burn records — Malaysia can exert formidable economic, market, and regulatory pressure without infringing on foreign territorial sovereignty.

Additional legal reform proposals put forward by civil society groups include amending Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution to explicitly recognise the right to a safe, clean, and healthy environment, as well as enacting a comprehensive clean air act.
Concurrently, the Education Ministry could elevate its haze guidelines into enforceable administrative regulations that prescribe mandatory minimum indoor air quality standards for classrooms.
The arrival of the northeast monsoon around mid-October typically clears the immediate skies.
However, until Malaysia enacts legislative reforms capable of addressing cross-border pollution, every dry season will bring the same public health crisis and the same jurisdictional limits.

* Dr Mohd Zulfakar Mohd Nawi is a Senior Lecturer at the Department of Professional Education and Postgraduates, Faculty of Technical and Vocational Education, Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM). Redza Zakaria is the Head Unit of Maritime Law, Policy and Governance at the Institute of Ocean and Earth Sciences (IOES), Senior Lecturer at the Faculty of Law, Universiti Malaya, and a member of the Group of Experts for the Ocean Literacy (WESTPAC) under Unesco.

He warned that alliances built solely for political survival would fail.
"The previous Muafakat Nasional charter served as the foundation, and now is the time to revive unity between both parties.

f183b62243f7ae76: PETALING JAYA, Oct 16 — The name Nancy Don Theseira Kitchen might not be familiar to diners.
Behind the scenes though is Don Daniel Theseira, better known for his previous business venture, Uncle Don’s.
Forty years in the F&B industry is nothing to sneeze at and Theseira flexes his muscles at his own no frills venture that opened in the quieter Taman Mayang Jaya.
He needs all that experience because the area is peppered with so many Western food eateries that a diner can hop around to find something to suit his/her wallet.
The secret weapon here is their array of Melaka Portuguese curries with a stray Filipino Sisig.
Their Western food isn’t the run-of-the-mill items either.
Take the Grilled Pork Chop (RM17.80), for example.
It’s a notoriously difficult item that I often avoid because it’s frequently dry or tasteless, making me prefer staking my chances on something safer like Chicken Chop.
Their approach is very chef-like: pounding it to a thinner piece. Less time on the grill means it retains a juicy texture.

For those worried about being shortchanged when it comes to the portion size, this isn’t the case; you’ll shudder if you’ve ever tried chewing a thick, stringy, dry pork chop that sticks to your teeth.
Another layer of sauce is brushed on top of the grilled meat giving it a light flavour. Black pepper sauce is available should you wish for a stronger taste.
Commercial French fries also win, as they are cooked to a golden perfection.
Fries and a juicy pork chop are a recipe for a clean plate.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sisig is great with alcohol or paired with rice as you get a mix of textures from the finely diced pork and pig’s ears mixed with the egg. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Sisig (RM18.80) was a new one for me since I have never eaten it before.
You can’t say no to finely diced pork with a little crunch from pig ear cartilage combined with a freshly cracked egg on a hotplate.
There’s a touch of zing from the calamansi lime and a smidgeon of spiciness from finely chopped red chillies.
I also spotted some stray strands of carrots and diced greens for health.
What interested me most were their curries. Portions are sized more for solo diners and meant to be eaten with rice.
It turns out there are clear winners that run out quickly, like the Wild Pork Curry (RM18.80) and Pork Leg Vindaloo Keluak (RM19.80).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Salmon Mango Curry is kept warm in a small claypot; it has a thick curry with tangy mango pulp and a piece of salmon. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
I ended up with a Salmon Mango Curry (RM30.80) served in a hot claypot with rice, a fried egg, lettuce, cucumber and fish crackers.
The thick curry has tangy, spicy hints, and the soft mango pulp pairs well with rice.
Wild Pork Curry is spicy on the tongue with a thick curry mixed with tender pieces of pork including a stray pork belly slice.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Wild Pork Curry is a thick, spicy curry with tender pieces of pork. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Pork Leg Vindaloo Keluak may look watery but the collagen in the pork leg turns into wobbly jelly after a night in the chiller.
The keluak flavour is definitely present but remains in the background behind the mild spiciness.
This one is more for those who like gnawing on bones to get to the skin and meat clinging to the pieces.

Pork Leg Vindaloo Keluak has a hint of the ‘keluak’ paste and one needs to gnaw on the bones to get the meat and skin. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Pineapple Prawn Sambal (RM18.80) is mildly spicy with small, bouncy prawns, mixed with a touch of sweetness from the pineapple.
Other choices include Pong Teh, a Melakan classic with soybean paste, the fiery Devil Chicken Curry, Rendang (pork or chicken) and even Asam Pedas Fish, a favourite for those who live in Melaka.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Prawn and Pineapple Sambal is spicy and sweet, featuring bouncy small prawns and pineapple. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi

There’s nothing fancy here; it’s just a neighbourhood place for families to get a good Western meal, sharing Bacon Nachos while they wait for pizza, a burger, or their choice of pasta or grilled meat.
Alternatively, one can relax and wind down with munchies like fried luncheon meat, pigs in a blanket (sausages enrobed with bacon), or just chicken wings.
Judging from the wall display, those who pledge their loyalty to the Liverpool football team will find another fan here.

a47d7870af952bac: PETALING JAYA: An NGO that advocates for migrants and refugees has criticised the health ministry’s proposal to mandate health insurance contributions for refugees and asylum seekers, describing it as unrealistic and inequitable.

Tenaganita executive director Glorene Das said refugees are not legally permitted to work in Malaysia, forcing them to rely on irregular incomes and leaving many unable to meet even their most basic needs.
Das acknowledged the existence of the Refugee Medical Insurance (Remedi) scheme, which provides coverage at about RM183.60 per year, but stressed that even this amount is too costly for refugees.

“How can we make insurance compulsory for people whom we do not legally allow to earn a living? We cannot deny refugees basic rights while expecting them to fulfil financial obligations,” she told FMT.
Das said the government should first evaluate existing mechanisms like Remedi, identify gaps in affordability and coverage, and explore how such schemes can be strengthened.

She said a more sustainable solution would be to first grant refugees the legal right to work in Malaysia, enabling them to afford their own healthcare while simultaneously contributing to the local economy.

“We must also recognise that preventive healthcare and early treatment are far less costly than emergency interventions when people delay seeking medical attention because they cannot afford it,” she added.

Last week, the health ministry proposed making health insurance contributions compulsory for registered refugees and asylum seekers to help cover their treatment costs and prevent the accumulation of medical bill arrears.
Deputy health minister Hanifah Hajar Taib said this should apply to refugees and asylum seekers registered under the government’s refugee registration system, also known as DPP.
Hanifah said more than 80% of outstanding medical bills involve undocumented migrants and stateless persons.
Premiums must translate into real coverage

Separately, a health think tank said the health ministry must ensure that its proposal would lead to medical coverage for the community, citing recurrent issues involving insurance for migrant workers in Malaysia.
Galen Centre CEO Azrul Khalib said migrant workers are already required to have medical insurance to work in Malaysia, yet unsettled bills remained a continuous issue for them.
“Where does the money paid for their insurance go? Are these funds being used to provide the health coverage paid for?
“The problem is ensuring that the money from premiums paid actually goes towards the payment of medical bills,” he said.

Azrul said the proposal itself was not unrealistic, given the existence of Remidi, which is available to all refugees registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees until age 60. The scheme is backed by Allianz.

He said the health ministry should rope in an established insurance and takaful operator to handle the proposal, as this was the best way to manage contributions while giving refugees and asylum seekers access to the private healthcare system.
1e1d3117aa6464f4: PETALING JAYA: Sebuah NGO yang memperjuangkan hak migran dan pelarian mengkritik cadangan Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) supaya caruman insurans kesihatan diwajibkan ke atas pelarian dan pemohon suaka, dengan menyifatkannya sebagai tidak realistik dan tidak saksama.

Pengarah Eksekutif Tenaganita, Glorene Das, berkata pelarian tidak dibenarkan bekerja secara sah di Malaysia, menyebabkan mereka terpaksa bergantung pada pendapatan tidak tetap dan ramai yang tidak mampu memenuhi keperluan asas sekalipun.

Das mengakui kewujudan skim Insurans Perubatan Pelarian (Remedi), yang menyediakan perlindungan pada kadar kira-kira RM183.60 setahun, tetapi menegaskan bahawa jumlah itu juga terlalu tinggi bagi pelarian.

“Bagaimanakah kita boleh mewajibkan insurans kepada golongan yang tidak dibenarkan secara sah untuk mencari nafkah? Kita tidak boleh menafikan hak asas pelarian sambil mengharapkan mereka memenuhi kewajipan kewangan,” katanya kepada FMT.

Das berkata kerajaan sepatutnya terlebih dahulu menilai mekanisme sedia ada seperti Remedi, mengenal pasti kekurangan dari segi kemampuan membayar dan perlindungan, serta meneroka cara untuk memperkukuh skim sedemikian.

Beliau berkata penyelesaian yang lebih mampan adalah dengan terlebih dahulu memberikan pelarian hak untuk bekerja secara sah di Malaysia, sekali gus membolehkan mereka membiayai penjagaan kesihatan sendiri sambil menyumbang kepada ekonomi tempatan.

“Kita juga mesti mengakui bahawa penjagaan kesihatan pencegahan dan rawatan awal jauh lebih murah berbanding rawatan kecemasan apabila orang ramai menangguhkan usaha mendapatkan rawatan perubatan kerana tidak mampu membayarnya,” katanya.

Minggu lalu, KKM mencadangkan supaya caruman insurans kesihatan diwajibkan ke atas pelarian dan pemohon suaka berdaftar bagi membantu menampung kos rawatan mereka serta mengelakkan tunggakan bil perubatan daripada terus meningkat.

Timbalan Menteri Kesihatan, Hanifah Hajar Taib, berkata kewajipan itu sepatutnya terpakai kepada pelarian dan pemohon suaka yang berdaftar di bawah sistem pendaftaran pelarian kerajaan, yang turut dikenali sebagai DPP.
Hanifah berkata lebih 80% daripada tunggakan bil perubatan melibatkan migran tanpa dokumen dan individu tanpa kerakyatan.

Sementara itu, sebuah badan pemikir kesihatan berkata KKM mesti memastikan cadangannya itu benar-benar memberikan perlindungan perubatan kepada komuniti berkenaan, dengan mengambil kira isu berulang berkaitan insurans untuk pekerja migran di Malaysia.

Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif Pusat Galen, Azrul Khalib, berkata pekerja migran sudah diwajibkan memiliki insurans perubatan untuk bekerja di Malaysia, namun isu bil perubatan yang belum dijelaskan terus berlarutan dalam kalangan mereka.
“Ke manakah wang yang dibayar untuk insurans mereka disalurkan? Adakah dana ini digunakan untuk menyediakan perlindungan kesihatan yang telah dibayar?
“Masalahnya ialah memastikan wang daripada premium yang dibayar benar-benar digunakan untuk menjelaskan bil perubatan,” katanya.

Azrul berkata cadangan itu sendiri bukan sesuatu yang tidak realistik, memandangkan skim Remedi sedia ada yang terbuka kepada semua pelarian berdaftar dengan Suruhanjaya Tinggi Pertubuhan Bangsa-Bangsa Bersatu bagi Pelarian (UNHCR) sehingga usia 60 tahun. Skim itu disokong oleh Allianz.

Beliau berkata KKM sepatutnya melibatkan pengendali insurans dan takaful yang mantap untuk menguruskan cadangan itu kerana langkah tersebut merupakan cara terbaik untuk menguruskan caruman, sambil memberikan pelarian dan pemohon suaka akses kepada sistem penjagaan kesihatan swasta.
7a6024e1508a486a: PETALING JAYA: Anyone who has loved a large dog may have noticed the unfairness of it: Great Danes, Irish wolfhounds and other big breeds often seem to race through life, while much smaller dogs can remain sprightly well into their teens.
Scientists have long known that larger dogs generally live shorter lives than smaller ones. A new study, however, may help explain what is happening inside their bodies as they age.
According to research recently published in Science, larger dogs appear to show faster age-related changes in their DNA than smaller dogs.

The study from Arizona State University involved 894 dogs representing around 120 breeds and formed part of the long-running Dog Aging Project. Researchers were not looking for changes to the DNA sequence itself, but at chemical markers attached to DNA that help regulate how genes behave.
These markers naturally change with age, which means scientists can use them to estimate how biologically “old” an animal appears to be.
A biological clock that runs faster

Notably, the researchers found that these age-related DNA changes accumulated more quickly in larger dogs. In simple terms, two dogs may be the same age in years, but the cells of the larger dog may show signs of having aged more rapidly.

The researchers also found that dogs whose biological age appeared older than their actual age were more likely to die during the following two years. This suggests the measurements were picking up real differences in the ageing process, rather than simply producing an abstract laboratory number.

One particularly interesting clue involved sections of DNA known as transposable elements - stretches of genetic material that can move or copy themselves within the genome. Cells normally keep them under tight control, but that control can weaken with age.
According to Arizona State University, larger dogs showed stronger age-related changes around these regions than smaller dogs, suggesting that this loss of control may be one piece of the puzzle.
Researchers stress, however, that this does not mean these DNA changes are definitively causing large dogs to age faster. They may instead be one sign of a broader ageing process.

The pattern in dogs is especially interesting because it seems to go against what we see when comparing different animal species. Large mammals such as elephants and whales often live much longer than tiny animals such as mice.
But within the same species, larger individuals can sometimes age faster.

Dogs are a particularly useful example because centuries of selective breeding have created an enormous range of body sizes, from tiny Chihuahuas to giant breeds weighing many times more. Some very large breeds have average lifespans of around 10 years or less, while smaller dogs can often live well into their teens.
The new study suggests that this difference is reflected not only in lifespan statistics, but also in the ageing of their cells.
The researchers also found that male dogs showed somewhat faster molecular ageing than females, although the biological patterns linked to sex were different from those associated with body size.

The study does not provide a single, definitive reason why large dogs tend to die younger. Ageing is influenced by many factors, including genetics, body size, growth rate and disease risk; what this research does offer is another clue to how those factors may play out at the cellular level.
For dog owners, the broader takeaway is simple: larger breeds appear to age faster not just on the calendar, but within their bodies, too.

64e85cc64c54f404: NEW YORK: Google announced Thursday it will start displaying links to websites and articles more prominently and higher up in search results powered by artificial intelligence (AI), as brands and news publishers warn of a sharp decline in their traffic.
The Alphabet subsidiary began integrating more AI features in its search results over two years ago.
In May 2024 it launched AI Overviews, where Google generates summarised answers to search queries, rather than only showing links as it historically did.
Then in March 2025 Google added AI Mode, which opens in a separate window and provides a more comprehensive answer and more links than AI Overviews.
Now, contextual links will be featured "more frequently" and higher up in AI-generated search content.
Google will also expand worldwide its link "carousel", which are cards displayed directly below AI Overviews that show headlines with images for relevant articles.

The algorithm will prioritise articles from sites a user has previously identified as "preferred sources", and it will also be able to pull in content from relevant social media posts and other forums.
Google will also make links displayed at the end of AI-generated summaries "more engaging and prominent" for users who want to "dig deeper".
During its second-quarter 2025 results, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said that AI Overviews had more than two billion monthly users in over 200 countries.
Several studies have shown that replacing traditional search with AI summaries significantly reduces the rate at which users open the suggested links.
According to a report by consultancy Chartbeat, news website publishers saw a 40% drop in traffic coming from Google between July 2025 and July 2026.
In August, Apig, a group representing daily newspapers in France, alerted the Competition Authority that AI summaries were in breach of agreements reached with news publishers in 2022.
34d68c8b3649e435: WASHINGTON: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, under scrutiny over her legal credentials, seemed to acknowledge Thursday that she had failed the bar exam but argued she was accurate in presenting herself as a lawyer.

Appointed by US President Donald Trump, Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

But there is no evidence to suggest that the 41-year-old press secretary has ever passed the bar exam, required to obtain a licence to practise law in the US, after graduating from Pepperdine University with a law degree.

When questioned Thursday by conservative media outlet Real America's Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move with her husband to China.

"We just said, 'Let's take this time, and I'll take the bar and see what happens.' The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," she said.
In Beijing, Zacharia worked as a lawyer at a major Chinese law firm.
She explained that she didn't retake the bar exam upon returning to the United States due to the birth of her first child.

Zacharia said that "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer, not an attorney at law...and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," given her law degree and experience in business law gained in China.
"I was very careful how I executed this," she said.
The Campaign for Accountability, a political ethics organisation, on Wednesday called for the California Bar Association to launch an investigation.
"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a licence isn't puffery; it's a crime," the organisation stated in a press release.
Zacharia held her first White House press briefing on Tuesday with an unusually short press conference where she answered questions from three journalists.
She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, a loyal Trump supporter and often combative press secretary, who stepped down in August to care for her young children.
a7e3c30948a8e8d0: PETALING JAYA: Dr Akmal Saleh may be plotting to contest the Jasin parliamentary seat in the next general election (GE16), analysts say, after the Umno Youth chief hinted at not defending his Merlimau state seat in the upcoming Melaka polls.

Syaza Shukri of the International Islamic University Malaysia said contesting in the state seats of Sungai Rambai or Serkam would allow Akmal to broaden his support base across Jasin, potentially strengthening his prospects for a parliamentary bid in GE16.
Merlimau, Serkam, Sungai Rambai, Rim and Bemban are all state seats within the Jasin federal constituency.
Syaza said it was common practice for leaders of national prominence like Akmal to transition from state to parliamentary level.
"If he wins with a strong majority, Akmal and Umno could ask for Jasin since PAS only won the parliamentary seat with a slim 322-vote majority in the 2022 general election," she told FMT.

However, Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia cautioned that such a move could complicate relations between Umno and PAS, amid speculation that the two parties were exploring electoral cooperation ahead of GE16.
"Jasin is now a PAS seat, but at the same time, Umno will be looking to regain parliamentary seats in Melaka, which aren't many in the first place.
"If Umno insists on contesting Jasin, it could cause some issues in its relationship with PAS," he said.

Akmal has been one of the strongest proponents of an Umno-PAS alliance, promoting it as a vehicle for Malay political unity. He has even threatened to sit out the state polls if Barisan Nasional chooses to work with Pakatan Harapan.
On Wednesday, the Melaka executive councillor hinted at leaving Merlimau to contest another seat in the upcoming state polls, suggesting that he may run in Serkam or Sungai Rambai.
The Star later quoted sources as saying BN had agreed to make way for PAS in Merlimau, with the Islamic party to field the head of its Melaka chapter, Zulkifli Ismail.
Sungai Rambai and Serkam are Umno strongholds that have never left the party’s grasp, although BN retained the latter with a very slim majority in 2021.
BN won Serkam in a four-cornered race, beating the Perikatan Nasional candidate by 79 votes, with PH and independent candidates left trailing far behind.
Akmal was elected Merlimau assemblyman in 2021 with a majority of 3,248 votes.
Melaka goes to the polls on Nov 14, with nomination day scheduled for Oct 31.
41403b85f386370d: PETALING JAYA: You've probably seen it lately - the sky turns a dull grey, there is a faint smell of smoke in the air, yet runners are still out on jogging tracks.
With races and training continuing through haze season, it is worth asking whether trying to stay fit could sometimes mean taking on more risk than we realise.

Haze from vegetation fires carries tiny particles known as PM2.5, measuring 2.5 micrometres or less - about 30 times thinner than a human hair. These particles can travel deep into the lungs and reach the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the bloodstream.

Running increases that exposure because we breathe faster and more deeply than we do at rest. The longer and harder the effort, the more polluted air we take in, which makes prolonged outdoor exercise particularly concerning during poor air quality.

Haze exposure can cause coughing, wheezing, irritated eyes and shortness of breath, while also worsening asthma and other respiratory conditions. Children, older adults, pregnant women and people with existing heart or lung disease are especially vulnerable, although healthy runners are not entirely protected.

One useful illustration comes from a London study involving 119 adults aged 60 and above, who completed two separate two-hour walks: one along traffic-heavy Oxford Street and another in the cleaner air of Hyde Park. The group included healthy participants as well as people with chronic lung or heart disease.

After the park walk, lung function generally improved and blood vessels became less stiff, with some benefits still detectable about a day later. Following the street walk, those improvements were usually smaller, although the effect was not identical across every measure.

People with lung disease reported more wheezing and phlegm after the polluted walk, while those with heart disease reported more coughing. Healthy participants did not necessarily feel worse, yet breathing tests showed less improvement in lung function and poorer relaxation of the arteries compared with the park walk.

The pollution in that study came from traffic rather than haze, and the participants were walking rather than running. Even so, the lesson is useful: how you feel is not always a reliable guide to what polluted air is doing inside your body.

Over the longer term, particle pollution is associated with heart disease, stroke, chronic lung disease and lung cancer. One hazy run is not going to cause a lifelong illness, and science cannot put a precise number on the long-term risk from a single race - but repeated training in polluted air adds to cumulative exposure.
Know when to move the workout indoors
None of this means runners should stop exercising. Start by checking the Air Pollutant Index (API) at the station nearest you before heading out.

The health ministry advises avoiding outdoor activities when the API rises above 100, which is considered unhealthy. People with asthma or current respiratory symptoms should be more cautious and may need to stay indoors until readings improve further.

On hazy days, an easy treadmill session, stationary cycling or strength training in a space with cleaner, filtered air can keep fitness ticking over without adding unnecessary exposure. Indoor air matters, too, so keep windows closed when outdoor conditions are poor, use an air purifier with effective particle filtration, and avoid smoking or burning candles or incense indoors.

Air quality can change throughout the day, so waiting for a better window may make sense. Malaysia's intermonsoon period and the approach of the northeast monsoon may bring changing winds and more rain, but clearer skies are never guaranteed.
If coughing, wheezing, chest tightness or unusual breathlessness develops during exercise, stop and move to cleaner air. Persistent or severe symptoms should be medically assessed.
Race organisers have a role, too

Runners should not have to make these decisions alone, particularly during organised events. In 2019, the health ministry advised that outdoor sports events should be postponed when the API exceeds 100.
A sensible haze policy should set out postponement criteria before race day, monitor local readings before and during the event, and give medical teams a meaningful role in decisions.
Runners should also receive timely updates, fair withdrawal or deferral options, and clear emergency plans covering participants, volunteers and spectators.

Moving a run indoors or postponing a race is not giving up; it is training intelligently. A healthy running culture recognises that endurance matters, but so does knowing when the air itself has become part of the risk.
This article was written by Dr Faizul Haris Hatta and Dr Noor Artika Hassan, lecturers in environmental health at the Department of Community Medicine at International Islamic University Malaysia.

f01d189e282f995b: A pointed and loaded question has been raised about a minister’s decision to resign. Apparently, he has been doing his job well — “What is wrong with him? What is wrong with his work?”
The problem is corruption, theft (sakau) and misappropriation. Yet, the focus is on the future of a beleaguered secretary-general of a political party.
The party’s defeats in recent state elections speak for themselves, reflecting both the state of affairs within the party and the calibre of its leaders, whether ministers or otherwise.
It is perceived, rightly or wrongly, that the party has not been able to make much headway on issues central to its support base, notwithstanding some peripheral achievements.
Viewed in the light of the number of parliamentary seats it holds, this is most disconcerting.
Perhaps the resignation should be viewed through these lenses to gain a more holistic perspective, rather than through the narrow lens of self-serving political interests.

Doing one’s job well is not the sole criterion for maturity. One must appreciate the three branches of government — the executive, the judiciary and the legislature (Parliament). Above these is the monarchy, given that Malaysia is not a republic.
The judiciary examines the facts and determines whether a person has broken the law. It has the power to impose custodial sentences.

The Pardons Board, chaired by the monarch, exists to grant pardons to those found guilty. It operates according to its own rules and criteria governing pardons. Whether a pardon is conditional or unconditional is not the point. That is the crux of the matter.

Some have gone out on a limb to question whether the monarch is “obliged” to follow the views of the other members of the board, or whether the ruler has absolute discretion to decide on the type of pardon to be granted.

Section 40A of the Federal Constitution has been bandied about. However, one must also take into account how the courts have ruled on matters relating to this provision when decisions have been challenged.

One must appreciate that the Pardons Board is part of the broader institutional ecosystem. One cannot clap one’s hands in glee when one part of the ecosystem functions according to one’s wishes — especially when certain individuals are found guilty — only to turn against the system and declare, “I will resign”, when another part of the same system makes an “unwelcomed” decision.
One cannot have one’s cake and eat it too. Either one accepts the system in its entirety or exits it completely and seeks another domain where all one’s desires might come true!

It appears that the role of the Pardons Board has been politicised. This should not be the case. It is a matter of public record which political party the federal territories minister, who is a member of the Pardons Board, belongs to. Is there an ulterior motive or an unspoken desire to “have it my own way”?
This is highly disturbing. A pressure group comprising retired civil servants, along with several other social groups, is seeking the minutes of the Pardons Board’s meetings.
What purpose would this serve?

Perhaps these groups should redirect their attention to the internal investigation into former Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission chief Azam Baki over the issue of shareholdings. To date, the public remains in the dark about the scope and extent of the investigation, as well as whether any breaches have been identified.
We can debate the use of the word “shall” and whether it imposes a binding obligation on the monarch to follow the advice of the other members of the Pardons Board.

To some, the debate reflects disrespect for the monarchy, whose head chairs the board. It should be noted that the Constitution contains no subclause requiring the minutes of the board’s meetings to be made public or providing for the general public to debate their contents and propose an alternative course of action.

If it did, the monarch’s role would be rendered superfluous. The institution’s role within the broader ecosystem must be respected and appreciated. Decisions should not be challenged merely on the basis of political preferences.
If any minister wishes to resign, he should do so now. A conditional pardon has already been granted.

If there is chagrin and dismay, and one is unable to appreciate the institutional framework that allows for both convictions and subsequent pardons, regardless of the reasons, then resignation should be immediate.
The country is better off without leaders whose interests are so parochial.
As for other pressure groups, they should find something more worthwhile to do, especially if they comprise retired civil servants who receive handsome pensions funded by taxpayers.
Let us not engage in political gymnastics by postponing a resignation until the day a house-arrest arrangement or other conditions come to pass. Move on and prepare for GE16.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

b2b1a540ac4f44d3: BUTTERWORTH: Kiru Muniandy has spent much of his life making things with his hands. He has painted portraits, carved ice and created elaborate hotel decorations; later, those same hands steered motorcycles, drove his daughter to school, and helped build a life around family, work and charity.

Then came Parkinson’s disease. Diagnosed in January 2023 at age 50, Kiru remembers walking out of the consultation room in tears, his thoughts immediately turning to his then seven-year-old daughter, Tammilina.
“I saw my future, my dreams and my plans crumbling down,” he recalled.

One memory cuts even deeper - when Kiru told his mother about the diagnosis, she held his trembling hands and said: “These hands were made to create beautiful paintings.” For an artist, the words struck at the heart of what Parkinson’s was beginning to take from him.
Kiru grew up in Kampung Jawa, Butterworth, and studied graphic design before painting portraits at Komtar during its heyday.

After his father died during the final years of his studies, Kiru, the eldest of four siblings, had to start earning a living. He eventually worked as a resident hotel artist before moving into manufacturing.

Outside of work, he and his wife Chitra supported charity events, including fundraisers for Hospice Penang. Kiru also loved motorcycles and helped co-found “No Ride Ends”, a Royal Enfield riders’ group involved in charity rides.
In 2019, the couple welcomed Tammilina. Like many fathers, Kiru imagined years of school runs, outings and family trips ahead.

Around the same time, something was beginning to change. He experienced unexplained anxiety, lethargy, constipation and internal tremors, while his left thumb twitched and fingers sometimes locked for weeks.
His shoulder began to droop and his left arm stopped swinging normally when he walked.
The answer finally came after he was hospitalised with chikungunya in December 2022. A doctor noticed the shaking in his hand and leg and referred him to a movement-disorder specialist.
Losing the ordinary things

Parkinson’s has since altered nearly every part of Kiru’s day. He can no longer drive alone or ride his motorcycle, struggles to walk for more than about 10 minutes, and experiences tremors, cramps, dyskinesia and dystonia - jerky movements and involuntary muscle contractions.
At times his body freezes, his speech can become slurred, and simple tasks such as dressing, pouring water or using the toilet require Chitra’s help.

His medication is taken every four hours and, when it works well, Kiru can regain some independence. When it does not, the gap between the man he once was and the life he now leads becomes painfully clear.
Losing the school run has been especially difficult. “I cannot give that memory to her, of being driven around by her own father,” he said.

Chitra has adjusted her working hours so she can care for Kiru while continuing to take their daughter to school and keep the household going. Kiru stopped working last October and is now on prolonged illness leave, with his income and benefits gradually reducing.
His applications for Socso invalidity pension have been rejected twice, and he is waiting for a medical report from the government hospital to support his latest appeal.
A possible second chance

In July 2025, after increasing doses of medication began causing troublesome side effects, doctors advised Kiru to consider deep brain stimulation (DBS). The procedure involves implanting electrodes in the brain to help regulate abnormal movement signals associated with Parkinson’s.

It does not cure the disease, but for suitable patients it can improve symptoms and reduce reliance on medication. Kiru has undergone assessments and has been told he appears to be a promising candidate.
The cost, however, is a challenge: DBS at Penang General Hospital is estimated at RM120,000, while treatment at a private hospital could cost around RM240,000.
Kiru is hoping for surgery as early as December, but he remains among other patients waiting for the procedure and worries that further delays could complicate matters as his condition progresses.
Friends, relatives and strangers have helped raise about RM32,000 through KitaFund, GoFundMe and personal donations, but the family is still a long way from the RM120,000 target.

For Kiru, the surgery represents far more than improved movement: he wants to walk more confidently, spend time outdoors with Chitra and Tammilina, and reclaim some of the everyday fatherhood Parkinson’s has interrupted.
Most of all, he wants to paint again. “If I can have the DBS, I hope I can do a big portrait painting of Tammilina,” he said.
“I tried my best, with or without Parkinson’s, to be a better father and a better person. My daughter is teaching me both. I love her.”

Kiru knows he cannot return to the life he had before Parkinson’s. What he wishes for now is enough time, movement and independence to create a few more memories with his daughter - and, hopefully, one more portrait she can keep.
Those wishing to help Kiru can contribute to CIMB Bank account 7020 495 568 (Kirubananthan a/l Muniandi) with the reference 'Donation for surgery'.
Donations can also be made through his KitaFund campaign or GoFundMe campaign.
This article was originally written by Fa Abdul.

45a485615a8cc732: KUALA LUMPUR: Amendments to current laws to allow the seizure of assets of alcohol- or drug-impaired drivers who fail to compensate their victims must have clear procedures for identifying, valuing and recovering such assets.

Universiti Putra Malaysia Road Safety Research Centre head Associate Professor Dr Law Teik Hua such procedures must also protect third parties and allow offenders to challenge seizures they considered excessive.
He said judicial discretion would also be necessary to assess offenders' actual financial circumstances and distinguish genuine hardship from attempts to evade payment.

He said the government should establish a formal compensation mechanism within criminal proceedings, with courts determining the amount payable based on the severity of the crash, damage incurred and the circumstances of each case.
Law proposed requiring offenders to declare their assets, setting realistic payment schedules and deadlines, and introducing enforcement measures to ensure compliance.

Law was responding to Transport Minister Anthony Loke's statement in the Dewan Rakyat earlier that the government was formulating a mechanism to seize assets and impose additional jail terms on drunk or drug-impaired drivers who failed to pay compensation to crash victims or the families of those killed.

Loke said the measures were intended to ensure compensation orders under amendments to the Road Transport Act provided meaningful recourse, particularly when offenders claimed they could not afford to pay.
He said the Transport Ministry planned to table the amendments in Parliament early next year.
Law said both the seizure of assets and the additional jail terms must be applied together if the amendments were to work.
He said this was the only way to strengthen enforcement and deter offences, while at the same time ensuring that victims, or their families, were compensated.

He said asset recovery could provide financial restitution to road crash victims and the families of those killed, while additional imprisonment would punish offenders who failed to comply with court orders.
"Relying solely on longer jail terms might not ensure victims receive the compensation to which they are entitled.
"The policy effectiveness of proposed amendments hinges critically on whether asset recovery will supplement punitive sanctions."
Law said asset seizures could be effective against offenders with sufficient financial resources and identifiable assets, helping address claims that they could not afford to pay.

"However, determining whether an offender is genuinely unable to pay could prove challenging, particularly when assets are transferred to third parties, ownership is concealed or properties are jointly owned."

He said the government should also consider establishing a victim compensation fund to provide provisional payments to affected victims and bereaved families while authorities pursue the recovery of offenders' assets.
"Insurance companies should also coordinate their payments with the compensation process to avoid duplication and minimise delays."
9c965add4bc82e1d: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 16 — How much will you be able to save in taxes in Malaysia, based on the proposed new income tax rates and individual tax relief in Budget 2027?
But first, very quickly, take a look at how the government proposes to change the income tax rate from 2027 onwards:

The main changes include reducing the tax rate for the chargeable income band of RM70,001 to RM100,000 from 19 per cent to 18 per cent, and reducing it for the RM100,001 to RM150,000 band from 25 per cent to 24 per cent.
What it means for you in ringgit and sen
To calculate how much tax you will be paying, take your total income in 2027, and then subtract the tax reliefs you will claim, which leaves you with the “chargeable income”.

Since Malaysia uses a progressive tax system, the tax you have to pay will be based on the different tax rates for the different income bands in your overall chargeable income, instead of one flat tax rate for your entire chargeable income.
So based on the proposed new tax rates for 2027, you could save RM300 or RM800 in tax, if your chargeable income is for example RM100,000 or RM150,000.

If your chargeable income is RM2 million, you will have to pay RM19,200 more in taxes, as the higher tax rate of 30 per cent is proposed to kick in earlier when the chargeable income exceeds RM1 million.

On Deloitte Malaysia’s website, its tax leader Sim Kwang Gek in her Budget 2027 commentary noted that the proposed 30 per cent tax rate (starting from above RM1 million instead of only to above RM2 million) appears aimed at partially offsetting the lesser revenue from middle-income taxpayers due to their lower tax rates, while ensuring higher-income taxpayers contribute more to the government’s overall tax revenue.
“The proposal therefore reinforces the progressive nature of Malaysia’s personal income tax system by shifting part of the tax burden towards those with a greater ability to pay,” she said.
Wait, there’s more: Taxpayers could save up to RM1,600 when lower tax rates are combined with higher tax relief

The individual tax relief, which is automatically given to taxpayers, will be raised from RM9,000 to RM12,000 from tax assessment year 2027 onwards. (This is the first time it has been raised since 2010).
That means you will automatically see an additional RM3,000 being deducted from your chargeable income, which ultimately means you will be paying less tax.
Here’s what this means, based on our own calculations using hypothetical figures for illustration purposes and also Deloitte’s examples:
• You will pay RM840 less in tax

(If your chargeable income would have been RM100,000 based on the RM9,000 tax relief figure, but it was pushed down to RM97,000 based on the RM12,000 tax relief figure. And also based on the proposed lower tax rate of 18 per cent for RM70,001-RM100,000 band, as compared to the current higher tax rate of 19 per cent for this band.)
• You will pay RM1,520 less in tax

(If your chargeable income is reduced from RM150,000 to become RM147,000, due to higher tax relief of RM12,000. Lower tax also due to proposed lower tax rates for the chargeable income bands RM70,001-RM100,000 (18 per cent) and RM100,001-RM150,000 (24 per cent), as compared to current tax rates.)
That’s more cash in your pocket, or more disposable income left for you to spend, save or invest.

So this is why Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said in his Budget 2027 speech that the combined effect of the higher tax relief and lower income tax rates would give an additional disposable income of up to RM1,600 to approximately five million taxpayers.
Of course, this is before factoring all the other tax reliefs you may be claiming, so the total tax you would be paying could be even lesser.

Do remember that all these proposed new income tax rates and higher tax relief is for tax assessment year 2027 and onwards, which means they are expected to only apply to the income you get in the year 2027 and the years after that.
5365e2bae4517879: RIYADH, Oct 16 — Mobile phones buzzed across central Riyadh with warnings of a “hostile aerial attack”, followed moments later by explosions and the sight of white plumes from interceptor missiles streaking across the night sky.
Yet, most residents have refrained from pulling out their phones to film such scenes, showing unusual restraint in a country where people routinely document and share everyday moments online.
Strict government warnings about filming those incidents appear to be working in the kingdom, with little footage or photos of strikes or air defences being posted.
Saudi Arabia has faced near-daily missile and drone attacks by Iran-backed Houthi fighters for more than 10 days.
The deadliest struck Riyadh airport on Saturday, killing 13 people and wounding 300 others in the worst attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.
In central Riyadh this week, foreign labourers yelled and pointed at the sky as interceptor missiles flew overhead, an AFP journalist saw, while many Saudis nearby remained stoic.
“It was a tense and frightening situation. We heard the explosions and saw the missiles on the horizon,” a witness who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue told AFP.
“It was a frightening moment that does not happen often, but it did not occur to me to film it because of the instructions,” he added quietly.
In Saudi Arabia, where over 60 per cent of residents are under the age of 30, apps such as Snapchat, TikTok and X have long been popular.
The kingdom’s interior ministry has repeatedly warned residents against filming and publishing images of drones, missiles, air defence interceptors and the impacts of barrages.
“Filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability,” read frequent messages from the ministry shared online.
Five people were injured earlier this week after debris from interceptor missiles fell over the capital, according to civil defence authorities.
But beyond images released by the authorities, photographs of the incidents have not been widely circulated online.
Meanwhile, other Saudi social media users have swarmed online platforms, slamming news organisations and journalists who publish reports they consider damaging to the kingdom.
Residents have also joined in the campaign by flagging incidents and informing authorities of foreign residents that may be harbouring sympathies with the Houthis.
‘We are being cautious’

Washington said this week that US citizens had been detained in Saudi Arabia after taking photographs of incidents involving attacks, without giving details on how many had been detained or whether they remained in custody.
Foreign residents have also told AFP that people they knew had been arrested after taking photographs or videos and posting them online.

In the capital’s gleaming new metro, the simultaneous buzzing from warning messages sent to mobile phones triggered visible anxiety among some passengers on Sunday evening, according to an AFP correspondent.
But despite the tension, no one spoke or attempted to discuss the ongoing attack with other commuters.
“Yes, we are being cautious,” said one resident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
“Of course we discuss what is happening because it affects our daily lives, but we do so in a low voice. We know that talking about these issues right now causes problems.”
For weeks, most Houthi strikes have targeted infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital or Riyadh airport.
But in recent days people in Riyadh are now hearing powerful explosions that sound much closer to the city centre.
The capital’s chronic traffic congestion has also appeared noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning was introduced in all schools and some companies ordered employees to work from home.
At the same time, life has gone on, with some restaurants and shopping centres still packed with customers.
“We hear and obey the leadership,” Saudi national and photography enthusiast Naif told AFP while showing off his new iPhone.
“If they say no filming, we will not raise our phone cameras.” — AFP

9a2bf2ad6c61ec11: ULAANBAATAR, Oct 16 — Inside a traditional Mongolian ger in the sprawling suburbs of Ulaanbaatar, children queue to have their teeth checked at a mobile dental practice that roams the vast country, providing treatment that is hard to come by in remote areas.
Hundreds of thousands of children in Mongolia suffer from untreated dental problems due to the combination of readily available sugary drinks and processed foods with a lack of dental care.

But the Misheel Kids Foundation (MKF) and its fleet of mobile dental clinics are seeking to address that, braving huge distances and frigid temperatures to provide oral healthcare to both the capital and far-flung communities.
“It was helpful that the dentists came today and actually showed us how to brush our teeth properly,” Agimaa, a 14-year-old girl, told AFP during one of MKF’s visits to an orphanage in the capital.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Members of the Misheel Kids Foundation (MKF) prepare a mobile dental clinic inside a traditional Mongolian ger in Ulaanbaatar. — AFP pic
“If someone doesn’t teach us, we don’t necessarily know how to do it ourselves.”
“It was very nice because I had a toothache,” eight-year-old Altanzul told AFP after receiving care.
Around nine out of 10 children across Mongolia have tooth decay, according to the charity’s paediatric dentist and project manager Namuunaa.
“We are facing a very serious situation,” she told AFP at the NGO’s dental facility in Ulaanbaatar.
Since the Soviet-allied communist era ended more than three decades ago, diets in the landlocked country sandwiched between Russia and China have changed dramatically.
Traditionally nomadic, the population of 3.6 million has rapidly urbanised.
Consumption of meat and dairy products, central to Mongolia’s herder heritage, is now complemented by the sweet, tooth-decaying snacks and sodas found in shops across the world.
But many children, particularly in the underprivileged suburbs of Ulaanbaatar, are not taught basic oral hygiene by their parents or schools.
And although dentists are more widely accessible in the capital, Namuunaa said “demand is much higher” in rural areas.
Children there “may simply have to live with the pain,” she said.

Namuunaa, who like many Mongolians goes by one name, participates in the NGO’s regular “dental treks” across the country, offering free examinations and treatment in places where such health services are limited or nonexistent.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Children learn about oral hygiene in Ulaanbaatar. — AFP pic
‘Smile’
Misheel Kids Foundation was founded by Swiss dental hygienist Gabriella Schmidt-Corsitto, who was shocked to see such high rates of childhood oral health issues in Mongolia.
“In every shop you go, it doesn’t matter how far from Ulaanbaatar... you find lots of sugar,” Schmidt-Corsitto told AFP.
To make matters worse, many parents are not aware of the consequences of constant sugar intake and do not teach children to regularly brush their teeth, she said.
“These two facts are, together, a disaster.”
Named using the word for “smile” in Mongolian, MKF has spent more than a decade trying to cultivate better oral health habits and so far has treated more than 22,000 children, Schmidt-Corsitto said.
The NGO’s newly established dental health centre is in one of Ulaanbaatar’s sprawling and underprivileged suburbs known as “ger districts”, named after traditional nomadic dwellings.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Children arrive to have their teeth checked at a mobile dental clinic inside a traditional Mongolian ger in Ulaanbaatar. — AFP pic
They offer dental services, training sessions for participants to become trainers themselves and regularly visit orphanages and daycare centres.
Alimaa, a mother of five children, spoke to AFP after a training session on oral health at the facility.
Hailing from the central-western province of Arkhangai, Alimaa said she “never went to dental clinics” in her hometown.
However, when she was a child, she said sweets were “not very common”.
Now, Alimaa said instead of the soft drinks and sugary snacks that her children might find at other people’s homes, she prefers serving them aaruul, a traditional dried curd snack.
‘Dental treks’

MKF’s “dental treks” are handled by a fleet of medically equipped mobile clinics, offering services ranging from checkups and cleanings to more intensive procedures including root canal treatments and tooth extractions.
During the treks, “there are days when we see 50 to 80 children in one day”, said Namuunaa, the paediatric dentist.
“It can be physically and mentally exhausting, but when you see how much the children need the treatment, you feel that you have to keep going,” she said.
A majority of its funding last year came from European foundations and private donors, with other support provided locally as well as by the Mongolian government.
Securing funding is “constant hard work”, she said, noting that she is also seeking more support from Mongolian authorities.
“We are not able to support the whole country, but we are an example... which could be copied,” she said. — AFP
b3a07683dd31a285: DURBAN, Oct 16 — Gunmen opened fire on local government candidate Khethelo Mdluli outside his rural home as he was with his young children, one of a surge of suspected political assassinations ahead of South Africa’s polls next month.
The 40-year-old died in hospital at the end of August, with his family telling AFP they did not know why he was targeted.
“My brother was not a violent man,” said the family representative, Sifiso Mdluli.

Mdluli was running as a ward councillor for the veteran Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) in the November 4 local elections, seen as a test of support for the African National Congress (ANC) after it lost its national parliamentary majority in 2024.
“One of his IFP colleagues, who was speaking at the funeral, said he had alerted them that there were people threatening him in the days leading to his murder,” his brother said.
The day after Mdluli died, another IFP ward council candidate was gunned down in broad daylight after arriving home in the same province, the politically volatile KwaZulu-Natal.
“He was a good man. We are scared,” said a relative of 34-year-old Lucky Sokhela who declined to be identified for fear of reprisals.
The party called a special Political Killings Task Team (PKTT), established in 2018, to investigate.
“The killing of political candidates cannot be treated as ordinary criminality,” it said. “Let the ballot, not the bullet, decide.”
In a new killing this week also referred to the PKTT, four members of the ANC youth division died after a gunman opened fire on them on Tuesday outside Johannesburg.
The motive was unknown and the attacker had turned himself in, police said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A car is set alight after clashes erupted between protesters and foreign nationals in Durban on October 8, 2026. — AFP pic
A tender, ward, job
At least 43 people were killed in 45 suspected political attacks in the first nine months of this year, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime (GI-TOC).

The tally topped the full-year total of 30 for 2021, the year of the previous municipal elections, and 33 in 2024, when the last national election was held, the independent civil society group said in a report.
The targets included ward councillors, party officials or traditional leaders — figures with influence over local issues such as the allocation of houses and contracts.

“The focus shifted from ideological divides to contestation over access to resources,” said researcher Crispin Hemson, who documented KwaZulu-Natal’s bloody political wars in the final years of apartheid.
“The market for killing, the networks, the guns, they were already there. Now the ideology is gone and the motive is a tender, a ward, a job,” he told AFP.

The trial of two men sentenced to life imprisonment in September for the 2023 murder of KwaZulu-Natal Democratic Alliance councillor Nhlalayenza Ndlovu heard the hit was ordered by a traditional chief over disputed land sales and electricity connections.
‘Kill or be killed’
A ward councillor’s job comes with a salary of more than 25,000 rand (US$1,500) a month before allowances, according to government figures.
The official national unemployment rate is 33 per cent and the minimum wage is nearly 6,000 rand.
“The struggle for employment is such that many people see being a councillor as escaping poverty,” said Zakhele Ndlovu, political analyst and lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
“Hence there is such competition for councillor posts, with others prepared to kill or be killed in pursuance of this position.”
Most of the attacks (16) recorded by GI-TOC to the end of September were in KwaZulu-Natal but there were also 10 in Gauteng, where Johannesburg is situated.
Of several political movements affected, most of those killed (13) were from the ANC followed by eight from former president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP), based in KwaZulu-Natal.

“Quite a few of these killings speak to the criminalisation of politics, particularly at a local government level, where it’s about contestation for access to power and the money that comes with it,” the author of the GI-TOC report “Ballots and bullets”, Julian Rademeyer, told AFP.

There is an “intersection between politics and organised crime” that “damages the constitutional democracy that South Africa is”, GI-TOC executive director Mark Shaw told a public hearing in September. — AFP
72fbe35fa8e3b875: From Moaz Nair

When hundreds of thousands of Malaysian students wait anxiously for their SPM results, or their peers across the causeway scan the O-Level boards, they are told that they are being evaluated purely on merit.
Educational syndicates proudly market these high-stakes gauntlets as “criterion-based” — an absolute measure of what a student knows, independent of anyone else.
But behind closed doors, a very different statistical reality plays out.

Contrary to what has been assumed to be criterion-based, Cambridge IGCSE and O-Level systems do not use fixed score thresholds. Instead of a rigid “90% equals an A*” rule, Cambridge adjusts grade boundaries after every exam series based on the difficulty of the specific test papers.

While the system evaluates students against fixed learning criteria, it incorporates statistical screening to ensure fairness; if an exam paper is exceptionally difficult, the mark required for a top grade drops.
This flexible approach ensures that a grade reflects the same level of achievement from year to year, without placing strict quotas or caps on how many students can earn an A* (A-star).

Almost all major examination boards — including our own Examination Syndicate (Lembaga Peperiksaan) and Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) — quietly layer norm-referenced adjustments on top of raw marks.

Colloquially known as “grading on a curve” or “standard fixing”, this hidden mathematical machinery ensures that an “A” earned in an unexpectedly brutal exam year holds the exact same currency as an “A” from an easier year.
While it keeps national systems stable, this invisible balancing act is reaching a dangerous tipping point, triggering a global reckoning over student burnout and economic reality.
How the curve secretly rules the world
Different countries mask or embrace this statistical architecture in unique ways, shaping how students progress into universities and the workforce.
Malaysia’s SPM operates on a “standard fixing” model — a criterion-related, norm-referenced hybrid.
While strict subject rubrics exist, the exact raw score thresholds required to secure an A+, A, or A- shift dynamically year-by-year based on the national cohort’s overall performance curve.
In the UK, the Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulations (Ofqual) uses a policy called “Comparable Outcomes”.

By mapping the current batch of A-Level students against how they performed years ago on their childhood exams, they mathematically predict what percentage should get top grades today, adjusting the grade boundaries to match.
Singapore, in collaboration with Cambridge Assessment, maintains a fiercely competitive system where cohort distributions fine-tune final grades.
This ensures consistent standards across different generations of test-takers competing for fixed tertiary slots.

South Korea’s Suneung, a high-stakes eight-hour college scholastic ability test, completely discards raw scores for standard percentiles. Under Suneung only the top 4% of the entire country can ever secure a Tier 1 grade.
Similarly, Australia scales different subjects against one another to output the Australian Tertiary Admission Rank — a pure percentile rank from 0.00 to 99.95.

In the US, the College Board uses a process called “equating” for the college admission test, known as “SAT”. Instead of scaling you against the people in the room on test day, they map your performance against a universal “norm group” of historical test-takers to ensure a score of 700 means the same thing today as it did a decade ago.
A fundamental trade-off
The tension between norm-referenced and criterion-referenced systems comes down to a fundamental trade-off between institutional fairness and individual well-being.

On one hand, norm-referenced grading acts as a safety net. If an exam board accidentally sets an impossibly difficult Mathematics paper, the curve automatically drops the required mark for an “A”, protecting students from being penalised for the year they happened to be born.
It also provides universities with an incredibly clean, efficient filter to select top-tier applicants.
However, the dark side is a toxic, zero-sum environment. It breeds a culture where a peer’s failure directly benefits your grade.

Worse, it masks systemic educational failures. If an entire generation’s literacy or mathematical mastery drops due to prolonged disruptions, standard-fixing can hide the rot by keeping the national percentage of A’s completely stable.
Intentional or not, using standard-fixing as a political shock absorber risks severing the link between a student’s certificate and their actual, real-world proficiency.

When the curve is adjusted to ensure pass rates remain palatable, it acts less like an objective academic yardstick and more like cosmetic anaesthesia, hiding structural damage under a layer of predictable percentages.

Ultimately, centralised exam boards face an impossible mandate: they are asked to be absolute measuring tapes of human knowledge, yet they must function as traffic cops for a finite number of university seats and corporate slots.
By choosing the stability of the curve over the raw truth of student capability, our educational systems have sacrificed individual transparency for macro convenience.

Until we reconcile this contradiction, we will continue to subject hundreds of thousands of students to a game where the rules are hidden, the goalposts move, and a peer’s failure remains the secret ingredient to one’s own success.
The bell curve may keep the system level, but it is flattening the very minds it claims to measure.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

2deb8e88fd91276a: Kita tahu tiga hari lalu Hakim Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin di Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur menolak permohonan Najib Razak untuk tangguh hukuman penjara 15 tahun dan denda RM11.4 bilion yang dijatuhkan ke atasnya setelah didapati bersalah dalam kes 1MDB. Tentunya ramai dalam Umno tidak suka. Umno memang mengikuti rapat kes Najib dan setiap perkembangan yang tidak memihak kepada bekas presiden mereka diterima dengan sugul dan marah. Umno tetap mempertahankan Najib meskipun pelbagai peringkat dalam sistem kehakiman negara mendapati dia bersalah. Ini membawa saya kepada artikel ini, ditulis oleh kolumnis FMT Tajuddin Rasdi bertajuk 'Teori kenapa orang Melayu terima pemimpin perasuah'.
Penulisan Tajuddin mendapat reaksi seorang ahli Pemuda Umno bernama Salahuddin Hamzah. Beliau menolak teori Tajuddin. "Saya sangat marah dengan teori itu," kata Salahuddin.

Dalam menidakkan pendapat Tajuddin, beliau berkata persepsi terhadap rasuah berada pada tahap kemuncak susulan skandal 1MDB antara 2014 hingga 2018. Apa yang berlaku selepas itu? Umno-Barisan Nasional ditolak secara besar-besaran oleh rakyat selepas memerintah negara selama 60 tahun. Pada 2022 pula BN hanya memenangi 30 kerusi.

Seterusnya Salahuddin berkata (ini bagi saya amat menarik): "Bukankah ini jelas menunjukkan rasuah yang dipersepsikan berlaku ketika itu turut ditolak oleh orang Melayu?" Oleh itu saya pelik. Jika tahu rakyat termasuk orang Melayu tolak rasuah mengapa Umno terus-menerus mempertahankan pemimpin yang dilihat ramai sebagai perasuah?

Dengan menggunakan istilah 'persepsi', Umno masih anggap Najib tidak melakukan rasuah meskipun Mahkamah Tinggi, Mahkamah Rayuan, dan Mahkamah Persekutuan -- membabitkan sembilan hakim -- mendapati dia bersalah dalam kes SRC International.

Bak kata wartawan veteran, A Kadir Jasin, di Facebook tempoh hari. "Ada pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong Umno yang gembira teramat sangat dengan pengampunan diraja. Ada yang gembira hingga lupa diri, tetapi ada juga yang sedar bahawa pengampunan bekas presiden mereka menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut."

Kata Kadir, dalam kalangan pemimpin dan ahli Umno ada yang tidak peduli sangat dengan hal-hal bersangkutan undang-undang, moral dan harga diri. "Bagi mereka skandal penyonglapan duit 1MDB bukanlah isu besar."

Menurut Kadir, "yang rugi dalam saga ini, adalah rakyat jelata dan pembayar cukai. Untuk membayar balik hutang 1MDB sahaja sebanyak RM42.5 bilion duit awam telah dibelanjakan sehingga 30 Jun ini. Pada ketika rakyat jelata yang tidak bersalah dibebankan dengan berbilion-bilion duit 1MDB yang dicuri dan pelbagai kemelut ekonomi, pihak-pihak yang membuat angkara semakin dimanjakan."

Memang benar kata Kadir. Lantas saya ulangi apa yang saya sering nyatakan pada beberapa penulisan sebelum ini. Selagi Umno mempertahankan Najib selagi itulah rakyat termasuk orang Melayu akan terus menjauhi Umno. Meminjam kata-kata Kadir tadi "menyukarkan pemulihan parti tersebut".

805454dbc6e7f5a2: NOTTINGHAM, United Kingdom: Britain's Prince Harry and his wife on Thursday carried out their first joint engagement since their surprise move back to the UK in August, with Meghan telling wellwishers: "It's great to be back."

King Charles III's 42-year-old younger son and Meghan, 45 – who left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud – were greeted with cheers as they arrived in the central English city of Nottingham.
The couple then stopped to chat and joke with the crowd as well as pose for selfies, give hugs and accept flowers.
The quasi-royal visit potentially puts the pair at odds with Buckingham Palace over their status while living back in Britain.

The king made it clear in a letter released last month that their position was "akin to private citizens" with charitable interests rather than public figures and that they should not be addressed as his and her royal highness.

Known formally as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, the last time Harry and Meghan appeared together at a public event in Britain was when they attended the late Queen Elizabeth II's funeral in September 2022.
Meghan, dressed in a long burgundy winter coat and wearing her hair in a ponytail, at one point kissed a woman on the cheek after she presented her with a gift.
Harry, in a dark suit and open-necked white shirt, bent down to speak to one youngster and told the crowd it was "very nice" to see everyone.
The couple were in the city to visit three charities that support young people and local communities through music, film, sport and tackling food poverty.
FAMILY RIFT

Following a spectacular falling out with the rest of the royal family, Harry and Meghan have sought to build bridges with Charles – but they remain estranged from Harry's older brother and heir to the throne, Prince William.
King Charles meanwhile visited Wales, where he addressed the Welsh parliament.
Anti-monarchy protesters could be heard chanting "Not my King" and "Down, down, down with the Crown" as Charles and Queen Camilla arrived, according to reports.
Charles, who was known as the Prince of Wales until his accession to the throne, has long had a close association with the country, one of the four territories that make up the United Kingdom.
Harry and Meghan settled in California six years ago, but in a surprise move in August they returned to live in the United Kingdom with their two young children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.
