I believed that to understand what words mean, you actually need a physical body and life experiences as part of the process. So I revisited the philosophy-of-AI literature I had once been steeped in, which asks what fundamentally distinguishes the kind of system that large language models exemplify, in extraordinarily advanced form, from the kind of processing we humans engage in. I gave several presentations to my own graduate students trying to make the case that, even though AI seems so intelligent, it’s actually different in kind — and I could not convince them.  And I thought, I know the difference, but I’m having trouble convincing even myself of what it is. And that led me to ask, “Wait a minute: Is there someone or something that stands behind the words, a human responsible for what is being said?” That’s the thing this extraordinary new language machine doesn’t have.  Whether these systems genuinely understand language is actively debated. But even if you grant them all the comprehension you like, they still lack standing. The buck can’t stop at a thing, a software system, with nothing to lose. Q: The Bulletin piece has these interesting examples of civic feedback forums where it looks like there are real people saying things, and instead you have a barrage of comments from AI. How did you find some of these other examples in society where things go off the rails in this way?  A: After the release of ChatGPT, I started hearing a concern from people inside government who review public comments on proposed rules: a suspicion that not all of the comments were written by humans. My reaction was: That’s going to delegitimize this channel for public feedback. That was several years ago, but everyone now knows this is happening. Public comment is a pillar of democracy. You don’t just put a new rule in place. People need to have a voice and feel like they’ve been heard before a rule is imposed on them. If you skip that step, people don’t accept rules as legitimate. That’s why that process is baked into how America works. And that pillar just cracked, and by now, in my mind, it’s fallen over. Has anyone noticed? My sense is the people on the receiving end of these comments have quietly adjusted the weight they give to public comments. It was never perfect, but boy, now much of its value is being swept away.  I open my essay with this example: In 2017, the Federal Communications Commission received more than 22 million public comments on its proposal to repeal net neutrality rules, and the New York attorney general later found that nearly 18 million of them were fake. As I write in the essay, “That fraud was caught because it left fingerprints: templated text, duplicated phrasing.” But large language models erase the fingerprints. Now every comment can be fluent and different, and reviewers can no longer tell which ones express views that real people formed and stand behind. If you have enough of the stuff that’s fake — words that no one with a stake actually stands behind — it desensitizes you to what’s real. That filters back to the public, and people realize: If I take the time to express myself, they’re not even listening any more. Q: Could you say a little bit more about your point that we need people with “standing,” who will take “accountability” for all pieces of text, even when those bits of text are generated by AI?  A: In the legal system, standing is a formal idea: sometimes a case isn’t heard because the people bringing it don’t have standing. But informally we use that term all the time. I’m not trying to formalize standing in everyday life. Instead I’m asking:  What is the informal sense of the term, borrowed from the legal one, that we need to pay more attention to now? Here in New England, consider the open town meeting: The person who stands up to speak is generally expected to have standing, as someone from that town with a stake in what gets decided. And if it’s a stranger who drove from across the state, or from out of state, everyone’s like: Wait a minute, who is that? They’re not from around here. In general, there’s just enough friction and it’s costly enough to show up somewhere you don’t actually have standing, that it doesn’t happen much. Now LLMs and the current digital networked environment collapse those boundaries. We always took for granted that if someone has a voice, it’s because they have standing. They have some basis to be heard. We need to pay attention to this, and really consider how to design systems so that the people with standing are the ones who get heard.  The other idea I tried to develop is “answerability.” It isn’t formalized in law, but it’s baked into the legal process. If you have standing to give testimony, there you are, ready for cross-examination. You have to be able to answer for what you’re saying. And if you’re making a specific accusation about someone, you have to be willing to back it with facts. Standing and answerability have to travel together: The right to be heard comes with the obligation to answer for what you say. That doesn’t mean everyone has to attach their name to everything. I write in the Bulletin essay, “Privacy and answerability aren’t opposites. … An institution can verify a person and stand behind their words without exposing them.” To voice a view, you only need to show that a distinct, eligible person is speaking. An accusation asks more: Someone trusted, like a reporter, has to be able to know who is speaking. As I say: “Disclosure obligations should scale with power, and identity protections with vulnerability.” None of this means AI can’t help. AI can do a lot of the work inside the chain of accountability — drafting, summarizing, finding patterns. If someone with a stake in a rule uses AI to draft a comment, adopts it as their own, and is ready to answer for it, that’s legitimate, in this context. What AI can’t do is anchor the chain. There has to be a person at the end who stands behind the words. In the essay I lay out four design principles for building that in: “attributable authorship,” a “decomposed and inspectable process,” the use of “provenance as infrastructure,” and the need to “widen standing rather than concentrating it.” As I write, the “animating rule is that autonomy is permitted while unaccountability is not.” And the metric that matters most isn’t the efficiency gained by removing humans, but the number of people AI places into roles where they can answer for what they do. Q: There is a phrase in the documents of the Center for Constructive Communication, that we need things to move “at the speed of trust,” not at the “speed of tech.” And that implies really thinking about building up these systems. Could you just say a little more about what that phrase means to you? A: I learned that phrase when I was in Appleton, Wisconsin, with Katherine Cramer [of the University of Wisconsin], a longtime collaborator, talking with community organizers who were running “Dialogue across Divides” conversations there. They had hundreds of people involved. I thought I was developing technology tools with exactly that same purpose, and was so excited to see it. And I asked one of the people who ran that organization, “How fast did you scale this?” And he paused, and then he said, “At the speed of trust.”  And I took that to mean “slow.” Then I realized he was saying: For you, slow, because you haven’t yet earned our trust. And I’ve since learned that when you do have trust, things can move fast. So bringing in technology is really a process of engagement. It doesn’t work to say, “Trust us, we’re doing this because we think it’s for your own good.” People will turn to someone they already trust and ask, “Is this good for us?” And if that person says “Yes,” things can move fast. Look at what’s happening at the intersection of AI and society: The speed of AI and the speed of democracy are running on different clocks. Talk to people who work in democratic practice and they say, “AI must slow down, because democracy can’t move that fast.” Talk to people in AI and they say, “AI cannot slow down, democracy needs to speed up.” If we can’t get these two time scales in sync, we’re headed for a breakway situation, where AI gets deployed faster than democratic processes can respond, and decisions get made without the public. That’s starting to happen right now.  Q: We need people actively doing things to build dialogue and figure out how tech tools can interact with that. At the Center for Constructive Communication, you’ve done a few iterations of the center’s Real Talk initiatives to build civic dialogues, as well as the Youth Voices Initiative in school settings, and currently you’re working on the New Social Forms project. Could you say a few words about them?  A: The Real Talk effort represents the longest-standing thread in this work. A huge emphasis of our work has been developing better ways to listen to one another. We create a context that is always small — small is beautiful here — where people are willing to share authentically. And we have the consent architecture and the technology to reveal the larger patterns, and then share them. We’ve done this with hundreds of communities around the country. And closer to home, we’ve brought the same approach to our campus here at MIT through the realtalk@MIT program, with support from the Office of the President and the Office of the Provost, to help our community build a culture around dialogue and listening.  The second thing I’d emphasize is that we’ve been doing more and more work on deliberative processes and citizen assemblies, and on how to make them more accessible. What if a group of high schoolers says, “We have a real problem with our cellphone policy?” Suppose you want to have an assembly that brings students, teachers, and administrators together, not just to listen to people’s concerns but to make policy recommendations. So we did that. The center worked with a high school in New York City, where technology helped people reveal their preferences and differences and listen to each other. We’re also building answerability into the technology. A prototype called VoiceTrace, developed by PhD student Cassandra Overney in our group, links every output statement — a summary of what was heard in a listening process, or a recommendation coming out of a deliberation — to the specific voices behind it, so any claim can be traced back to the conversations it came from. The New Social Forms project pertains to a very interesting pattern emerging in workplaces around the world, certainly the ones we’re connected to. AI is an extraordinary tool for individual empowerment, but in the words of one of our collaborators at the Google Experience Institute, people are tunneling. They go deep, using AI to develop refined ideas, but when they surface, their ideas have diverged from their teammates’. So groups and teams trying to work together with AI, there’s a human coordination problem. We’re going to expand the initial work we’ve started with Google because there’s a lot of interest in collective communication, trust, and interaction among people trying to work together.  So is that a civic context? It’s a workplace, but workplaces are civic spaces, too. They govern people’s daily lives, they’re where many of us build civic skills and learn to cooperate across difference, and there’s a long tradition of civic life rooted in shared work. We’re all humans trying to interact with each other. These are the same issues. Justice Louis Brandeis once used the phrase “industrial democracy” to capture this. When workplaces lacked certain kinds of civic processes and civility — two interestingly related terms — labor disputes used to turn violent. Procedural justice, mediators, and people hearing one another are just as necessary in the workplace. In the end, it’s all about human beings. Hearing the humanity in one another is what democracy depends on, and it’s just as necessary for communities and organizations to function.
352ced96796d8926: From Azam Mohd
The 2027 budget raises a question Malaysians rarely ask: who bears responsibility when national promises reach citizens unevenly? The answer cannot rest with Putrajaya alone.

A budget becomes meaningful through state governments, local councils, schools, clinics and businesses. Malaysians should therefore judge this spending plan by whether public institutions can work together across administrative boundaries.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim tabled a RM460 billion federal budget on Oct 9. The finance ministry projects growth of 4.2% to 5.2% next year, while the fiscal deficit is expected to narrow to 3.3% of gross domestic product.
These forecasts are not guarantees. Their significance depends on what happens after Parliament approves expenditure and ministries begin implementation.
Consider the distance between a federal announcement and a household’s experience.

A parent may welcome education funding but still be confronted with an overcrowded classroom. A patient may hear about health allocations yet encounter long waiting times. A trader may qualify for financing but struggle with permits, infrastructure or inconsistent local enforcement.
Getting things done
None of these difficulties can be resolved by increasing appropriations alone. The missing ingredient is coordination.

Federal ministries design programmes, states control land decisions, and local authorities shape everyday business conditions. When their priorities diverge, public money can purchase activity without producing improvement.

The resulting frustration is often blamed entirely on whichever party governs nationally, although responsibility may be distributed across several institutions. This is particularly important for Sabah and Sarawak, where distance, infrastructure gaps and administrative arrangements complicate delivery. The same principle applies to rural districts in Peninsular Malaysia and densely populated urban neighbourhoods.

Equal allocations do not necessarily create equal access. A credible federal budget must recognise different costs and starting conditions without turning regional needs into partisan bargaining chips.

The 2027 budget also arrives amid uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict. Bank Negara Malaysia has announced additional financing support for smaller enterprises facing temporary cash flow pressures. Such measures can help firms survive disruption, but credit cannot repair a blocked supply route or eliminate higher transport costs. Businesses need agencies responsible for financing, logistics and trade facilitation to respond coherently together.
Delivering on promises

Malaysia, therefore, needs a delivery compact between federal and state institutions. For major programmes, the responsible ministry should identify the implementing agencies, milestones and obstacles. State governments should disclose the approvals and infrastructure commitments under their control. Local authorities should report service bottlenecks.
These arrangements would make responsibility visible without assigning every problem one political owner.

Parliament has an important role. Budget debates too often concentrate on announcements and partisan comparisons. Parliamentary committees should instead examine why comparable districts achieve different results with similar resources. Auditors can test whether procurement and implementation follow established rules, while elected representatives can question delays without alleging misconduct.
Poor performance warrants investigation; it is not, by itself, proof of corruption.

There are legitimate objections. Reporting can become bureaucratic, and states may resist federal conditions that intrude upon their constitutional responsibilities. The solution is not another elaborate national dashboard. It is a limited set of jointly agreed service standards, published responsibilities and independent verification, designed around programmes where fragmented authority obstructs delivery.
Out of the political fray

Political competition makes this more urgent. With the next general election approaching, governing parties will claim achievements while opponents highlight shortcomings. Both have legitimate democratic roles.

But citizens should be able to distinguish a policy that failed because of flawed design from one delayed by procurement, staffing, local approvals or unexpected external shocks. That distinction improves accountability rather than shielding ministers from criticism.

A useful starting point would be to select several high impact programmes spanning education, healthcare, small business support and regional connectivity. Publish who is responsible for each stage, invite state participation and review outcomes after implementation begins.
Where cooperation fails, disclose the disagreement and its consequences. Where it succeeds, retain the practice regardless of which coalition controls the relevant government.
The 2027 budget will ultimately reveal whether Malaysia can move beyond a culture in which announcing expenditure is treated as governing.

The country does not lack ambitious public promises. It needs institutions capable of delivering them together, especially when political loyalties differ. Fiscal credibility begins with sound numbers, but public confidence grows when responsibility is shared, visible and impossible to evade.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
23be0a5665a7f0e9: Dunia ini umpama sebuah penjara yang besar dan dipenuhi dengan segala macam hantu. Itu agaknya yang cuba disampaikan oleh Joko Anwar melalui filem arahannya, Ghost in the Cell. Saya tidak tahu apa genre paling tepat untuk filem ini. Komedi seram absurd barangkali tetapi dalam komedi ada serius dan misteri, ada keganasan, ada aksi ala kartun. Semuanya bercampur, mencetuskan kecelaruan. Joko mungkin mahu menyatakan yang hidup ini beginilah, penuh dengan kecelaruan ragam dan identiti. Malah ada babak yang mengarut sehingga saya teringat filem Kung Fu Hustle arahan Stephen Chow.

Filem Ghost in the Cell ini turut menampilkan dua nama dari Malaysia, Bront Palarae yang memegang watak Jefry, seorang pegawai penjara dan Ho Yuhang sebagai Rendra, seorang banduan yang merupakan ketua sindiket dadah. Ho yang lebih dikenali sebagai pengarah filem membawakan watak penjenayah bertubuh kecil tetapi cukup digeruni.

Cerita bermula dengan Dimas (Endy Arfian), seorang wartawan yang dituduh membunuh ketuanya lalu dihumban ke penjara Labuhan Angsana. Di situ dia bertemu pelbagai jenis manusia, termasuk Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya), seorang banduan yang sering membela orang lain walaupun tindakannya menyebabkan hukuman penjaranya bertambah. Watak Anggoro memperlihatkan satu paradoks. Dia memang pesalah di sisi undang-undang tetapi masih mempunyai rasa kemanusiaan yang tinggi. Sebaliknya, ketua penjara yang diberikan kuasa menjaga undang-undang pula bersifat binatang atau hantu dalam mengejar pangkat dan kedudukan.

Di penjara itu juga ada Tokek (Aming), banduan ganas yang menjadikan keganasan seksual sebagai alat menakutkan orang lain. Dimas yang baru masuk penjara menjadi sasarannya. Tokek mewakili manusia buas dan gemar membuli orang yang lebih lemah. Melihatkan wajahnya sahaja sudah cukup membuat kita menggeletar. Bagaimanapun, dia mati akhirnya setelah gagal mempertahankan diri apabila berhadapan dengan hantu yang ternyata lebih perkasa. Tokek adalah gambaran manusia yang sebenarnya tidaklah kuat mana tetapi hanya berani kerana dia tahu pihak yang dibuli itu sudah sememangnya penakut. Dia memanipulasi keadaan.

Apa yang menarik perhatian saya ialah cara hantu dalam filem ini membunuh mangsanya. Mayat mangsa disusun dan digubah seakan sebuah arca seni. Ini bagai satu metafora yang menarik. Ia tentang kita yang kadangkala menggambarkan keindahan dengan mempergunakan penderitaan orang lain. Arca memanglah cantik dan hebat tetapi ia dibuat menggunakan mayat yang penuh darah dengan isi perut yang terburai, biji mata terkeluar dan sendi yang patah. Manusia begitulah, mempergunakan hidup pihak lain demi mencari keuntungan dengan menjual gossip dan fitnah, hiburan atau berita buruk tentang mereka. Dan kita gembira menikmati keindahannya sebagai bahan tontonan tanpa mempedulikan kesengsaraan di sebaliknya.

Lebih menarik lagi dalam Ghost in the Cell ini ialah hantu yang membunuh itu akan menyerupai mangsanya sendiri ketika menyerang. Ia seolah-olah manusia itu akhirnya dibunuh oleh kejahatan yang terpelihara di dalam tubuhnya sendiri. Hantu bukan datang dari luar, tetapi dari dalam kita sendiri.

Satu lagi watak yang menarik ialah Six (Yoga Pratama), banduan yang tidak berpegang kepada agama tetapi mempunyai kebolehan melihat hantu dan aura manusia. Ini satu lagi paradoks. Selalunya orang alim yang lebih memahami perkara ghaib. Tetapi dalam filem ini, orang yang tidak beragama pula mampu melihat sesuatu yang gagal dilihat oleh orang lain. Saya melihatnya sebagai sindiran, kerana manusia tak kira apa bangsa atau agama pun tetap dikurniakan tuhan dengan kelebihan masing-masing tetapi adakalanya kelebihan yang diberikan itu tidak mampu difahami olehnya sendiri dan dia perlukan bimbingan. Maka itu, banduan alim bernama Wildan (Mike Lucock) diperlukan untuk mentafsir warna-warna aura yang dilihat oleh Six. Wildan tak mampu melihat aura yang keluar dari tubuh manusia seperti mana Six, tetapi dia mempunyai keilmuan untuk mentafsirkannya. Nah! Begitulah tahap manusia dalam memahami, mempercayai dan menghayati sesuatu. Faham, percaya dan menghayati adalah tiga perkara yang cukup besar bezanya.

Di dalam filem ini, tertarik kepada manusia yang mempunyai aura negatif seperti kemarahan dan kebencian. Untuk mengelakkan diri daripada menjadi mangsa, banduan perlu menenangkan fikiran dan mengawal emosi. Ada yang memilih untuk bersembahyang, ada pula yang menari. Sembahyang merupakan ritual yang menghubungkan manusia dengan tuhan, sedangkan menari lazimnya dianggap kegiatan hiburan. Tetapi dalam filem ini, kedua-duanya boleh menghasilkan ketenangan yang diperlukan untuk menghindari hantu. Yang hendak diperlihatkan bukanlah soal cara mana lebih suci atau lebih baik, tetapi bagaimana manusia mencari ketenangan melalui jalan yang berbeza. Maknanya, ketenangan hati itu penting biarpun kita berbeza pegangan. Tetapi di dalam dunia yang bernama penjara, mereka terpaksa mencari apa saja persamaan untuk terus hidup dengan selamat. Untuk selamat, manusia perlu tenang.

Kemudian kita diperkenalkan kepada Prakasa Kitabuming (Arswendy Bening Swara), seorang politikus dan ahli perniagaan berpengaruh yang menjalani hukuman penjara tetapi masih menikmati kemewahan. Dalam penjara yang sama, ada orang yang hidup berhimpit dan terdedah kepada keganasan, sedangkan orang tertentu masih boleh menikmati layanan istimewa. Sepatutnya apabila seseorang dihukum, pangkat dan kedudukannya tidak lagi memberikan keistimewaan. Orang biasa masuk penjara kehilangan kebebasan. Orang berpengaruh masuk penjara masih boleh bermewah-mewahan. Ada pula watak Sapto sebagai Ketua Penjara yang mempunyai cita-cita besar menjadi Menteri sehingga sanggup tersengih-sengih dan melutut demi membodek Prakasa, politikus yang menjadi penghuni penjaranya sendiri.

Sebenarnya hantu itu mahu mencari Prakasa. Hantu mengikut Dimas ketika Dimas meninjau kawasan hutan Kalimantan yang musnah angkara Prakasa. Tetapi, dalam usaha memburu Prakasa ramai yang menjadi korban. Prakasa menemui ajalnya dengan cukup sinis. Dia berhadapan dengan hantu yang menyerupai dirinya ketika muda, ketika dia konon masih seorang pejuang yang mempunyai cita-cita dan prinsip. Dia adalah gambaran pejuang muda yang telah mengkhianati prinsip perjuangannya setelah berada di puncak kuasa. Hantu yang membunuhnya adalah diri mudanya sendiri yang pernah berapi-api berjuang. Rupanya si pejuang ini telah menjadi tawanan kepada pangkat dan kuasa.

Ada satu babak, kita diperlihatkan dengan sekumpulan banduan artis dan selebriti yang diasingkan daripada kumpulan Dimas dan Anggoro. Dialog lucunya ialah ‘rakyat Indonesia lebih mengambil berat nasib artis daripada nasibnya sendiri'. Saya ketawa kerana sindiran itu bukan masalah di Indonesia sahaja. Kita di sini pun sama. Kita boleh bergaduh siapa betul siapa salah bila artis bercerai dan berantak, kita sanggup masukkan duit di dalam akaun bank pempengaruh media sosial yang mengadu perniagaannya bakal melingkup kerana hutang yang membebankan sedangkan apabila sepupu kita hendak menjual dodol buatannya sendiri, kita tak jawab WhatsApp dia langsung. Kita simpati kepada artis yang sedang sakit tetapi jiran sebelah sudah sebulan terlantar di wad, kita tak jenguk pun. Memang kita semua obses dengan artis dan selebriti.

Joko melihat penjara bukan sekadar set penggambaran dan premis penceritaan. Ia adalah dunia. Dunia boleh jadi syurga jika semua manusianya tenang dan damai tetapi dunia boleh jadi sebuah kurungan yang menakutkan jika di dalamnya bercampur antara manusia baik dengan manusia durjana. Di dalam filem ini digambarkan manusia ada yang mahu berkuasa, ada yang mahu dilindungi, ada yang mahu dipuja dan ada yang sekadar mahu terus hidup. Hantu adalah dosa silam yang memburu manusia itu sendiri untuk menghukum jika manusia tersebut masih tidak mahu berubah menjadi insan yang baik. Di tengah-tengah seram, ngeri, takut dan cemas itu kita masih ada ruang untuk ketawa. Sepertinya kita faham bahawa dunia ini hanyalah senda-gurau sementara sahaja.

Memang semenjak dua ini saya sering menulis tentang filem dan teater yang saya tonton. Ini kerana apa yang ingin saya sampaikan dalam tulisan berkenaan kehidupan telah berjaya dipersembahkan oleh mereka dalam bentuk visual. Saya tidak pastilah tafsiran saya menepati apa yang dimaksudkan oleh karyawan asalnya tetapi inilah yang boleh saya kutip untuk dikongsi bersama. Untuk kita renungi kehidupan ini melalui sebuah persembahan kreatif.

Sebuah karya yang sudah dipertontonkan kepada masyarakat tidak semestinya mempunyai satu tafsiran yang wajib dipatuhi. Kita bebas menterjemahnya. Apa yang saya lihat dalam filem ini adalah tentang perangai manusia yang terpenjara akibat menjadi mangsa kepada nafsu buas sendiri. Nafsu manusia memang tak pernah puas. Jika ada peluang untuk naik, manusia akan naik walaupun akan menindas manusia lain. Dari situlah wujudnya dendam dan pembalasan oleh pihak yang teraniaya. Hantu dalam Ghost in the Cell itu muncul pun kerana manusialah yang mengundangnya. Telah kita pelajari di dalam kitab al-Quran, manusia adalah sebaik-baik kejadian dan makhluk terbaik ini jugalah yang sedang menghancur-musnahkan dunia.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
d4e994a42990ef49: From Moaz Nair

The ghost of Malay politics past continues to haunt a fading Umno. Ever since its historic, humiliating downfall in the 2018 general election, the party has been trapped in a state of pathetic paralysis, desperately daydreaming about reclaiming its crown as the nation's undisputed political hegemon.

Yet, instead of executing a clear strategy, Umno's leadership is caught in a dilemma of cowardly choices: suck up to Pakatan Harapan in a volatile unity government, or venture into the wilderness alone, or crawl back to its treacherous former rival PAS.

This delusional "two-tier approach" – trying to play both sides by cutting different deals at the state and federal levels – is a weak political gimmick that has failed to fool anyone, least of all PAS.

Meanwhile, Umno’s relationship with PH has rapidly soured under its current leadership. By even flirting with PAS, a party that relentlessly trashes PH as secular and liberal, Umno is actively incinerating whatever fragile trust it has left with its current governing partners.
Let’s call a spade a spade: this is a desperate, toxic battle for survival.

After bloating itself on power for nearly six decades, Umno still blindly demands to be treated as the "Big Brother" of Malay politics. But wake up: PAS now holds the actual cards. Armed with a superior parliamentary seat count and total control over four state governments -- Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis -- PAS has effectively usurped the throne.
Walking into a trap

Analysts see right through Umno’s terror. The party knows that any formal alliance with the Islamic juggernaut will reduce Umno to the position of a weak, castrated junior partner. History has proven time and again that when these two egos clash over who commands Malay politics, a bloody political knife-fight is virtually guaranteed.
Besides, how short is Umno's memory?

The catastrophic collapse of the 2019 Muafakat Nasional pact should have been a permanent lesson. PAS didn't hesitate to stab Umno in the back, secretly conspiring with Bersatu to form Perikatan Nasional in 2020. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi openly branded that move a betrayal, and the party rank and file still rightly whisper that PAS carries a "DNA of betrayal".
To walk back into that trap is pure political suicide.

Any attempt at a reunion faces brutal realities: PAS will never surrender the safe, Malay-majority seats it currently locks down. It will greedily force Umno to run in highly volatile, hostile areas, guaranteeing an electoral wipeout of Umno's remaining footprint.

PAS’s aggressive youth wing and top leaders are no longer hiding their ambitions: they want a PAS prime minister. They will never yield the top job to a diminished Umno, shattering any illusion of an equal partnership.
Can Umno survive?

Umno’s traditional lifeline has always been its ability to bridge gaps using non-Malay votes. Crawling into bed with an uncompromising Islamist party will permanently alienate those voters, severing Umno's last remaining oxygen supply.

This desperate anxiety is already reeking at the state level. In Perak and Pahang, Umno leaders hold the posts of menteri besar only out of sheer charity by PH, not because Umno commands a real majority. Inviting PAS into these states is code for a hostile takeover. PAS will effortlessly leverage its momentum, hijack the state machinery, and relegate Umno to political irrelevance on its own turf.

PAS knows it doesn't need Umno; its most realistic path to absolute power remains firmly rooted in consolidating its Malay-Islamic framework. This leaves Umno stranded at a historic crossroads of its own making. Going solo in today’s fractured landscape offers zero guarantee of survival, yet leaping back into the arms of PAS ensures complete subordination to a green wave that has already captured the Malay-Muslim electorate.

If Umno wants to survive, it needs to snap out of its historical delusion. It can no longer demand the "Big Brother" crown based on past glory. It must adapt to a brutal new reality or get comfortable being buried in the footnotes of Malaysian history.

d4cc7aabe8176b8f: For decades, South Asia was locked in a perpetual cycle of conflict management: brief military clashes between India and Pakistan would be followed by de-escalation and the resumption of formal peace talks, which eventually gave way to another bout of conflict. But this pattern has now been broken.

No high-level dialogue has taken place since 2016. Rather than some temporary diplomatic tantrum, this reflects a paradigm shift in Indian foreign policy, permanently altering the subcontinent’s security architecture.

The roots of this stalemate can be found in the structural failures of past diplomacy. In 1947, 1965, and 1971, Pakistan initiated conventional wars, none of which delivered the results it desired. The third resulted in the breakup of the country and the birth of independent Bangladesh.

These experiences, together with the success of the US-backed mujahideen in their fight against Soviet forces in Afghanistan in the late 1980s, prompted Pakistan’s military to embrace a new strategy, based on asymmetrical warfare—or, more bluntly, terrorism.
From 1989 to 1993, as terrorist attacks caused significant civilian casualties in India, Pakistani officers crowed about “bleeding India to death by a thousand cuts”.
Indian leaders were nonetheless convinced that structured dialogue could persuade Pakistan to abandon this strategy. This belief gave rise to the Composite Dialogue framework in the late 1990s.
This bureaucratic mechanism was designed to segment contentious issues—ranging from Kashmir to trade and humanitarian concerns—so that friction in one area would not derail progress in others.
There was just one problem: every major Indian peace overture was met with an act of military or terrorist provocation that the Pakistani government was either unable or unwilling to prevent.

In 1999, when then-Indian prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee undertook his historic bus journey to Lahore to sign a landmark peace declaration, Pakistani troops were infiltrating the Kargil district of Ladakh—actions that led to the Kargil War (which Pakistan lost).

In 2008, when back-channel diplomacy was on the brink of delivering a non-territorial solution to the Kashmir issue, coordinated terrorist attacks by Pakistan-based militants killed 166 innocent civilians in Mumbai.

This cycle exposed a profound institutional disconnect within Pakistan. Its civilian governments lacked the authority or longevity to fulfill the commitments they made at the negotiating table, and its military-intelligence apparatus viewed peace with India as an existential threat to its domestic hegemony.

Now, India has had enough. Prime Minister Narendra Modi initially followed the old peacemaking script. He invited his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, to his 2014 inauguration, and visited Lahore the following year.
Even when this visit was followed by a terrorist attack on the Indian airbase in Pathankot, Modi invited Sharif to join the official investigation into the incident.
Then came the final straw: Pakistan’s joint investigation team concluded that the attack was a “drama staged by India to malign Pakistan”.

With that, India abandoned its doctrine of strategic restraint in favour of a new guiding dictum: talks and terror cannot coexist. India would return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantled, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

This diplomatic shift was accompanied by a fundamental change in India’s military doctrine. For nearly three decades, Pakistan assumed that its tactical nuclear arsenal would deter India from launching conventional military reprisals for terrorist attacks. Then India decided to call Pakistan’s bluff—most notably, in last year’s “Operation Sindoor”.

Through calibrated retaliatory actions, ranging from surgical cross-border strikes to sophisticated aerial bombardments targeting terrorist infrastructure deep within Pakistani territory, India demonstrated a willingness to accept escalation risks to impose tangible costs on its neighbour.
By signalling that state-sponsored terror would automatically trigger a conventional military response, India has sought to rewrite the rules of deterrence in South Asia.
The current stalemate is hardly desirable. The absence of a diplomatic safety valve between nuclear-armed neighbours poses acute risks to regional, even global, stability.

Even the most basic bilateral matters, such as humanitarian issues, trade blockades, and water sharing, are now viewed through a hyper-politicised national-security lens. And if a new crisis erupts, what mechanism is available to manage it? The margin for miscalculation is perilously thin.

But the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak. Pakistan’s military leadership still pins its domestic political legitimacy partly on hostility towards India, even as the country faces profound economic distress. And India, with its growing economic and conventional-military advantages, has little reason to compromise on its core security interests.

The US is certainly not encouraging India to rethink this stance. Not only has Donald Trump’s administration all but abandoned America’s Indo-Pacific strategy, in which India played a central role as a critical counterweight to a rising China, it has also embraced Pakistan, which, despite its financial instability and close ties with China, has managed to woo the US administration by striking a lucrative cryptocurrency deal with a Trump-linked firm and unctuously nominating Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize.

With the underpinnings of the India-Pakistan conflict firmly entrenched, the current stalemate should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate strategy of disengagement.

Until Pakistan undergoes a political transformation that fundamentally alters its security calculus, or a “black swan” event forces an existential realignment of regional priorities, the silence across the subcontinent will endure—and the risk of catastrophic error will remain.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and human resource development, is a fourth-term elected MP for the opposition Indian National Congress.

Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brad Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

7af8688e509420ee: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah

Last week, I attended a screening of Man Who Walked the Talk: The Tun Razak Story. As I watched his life unfold, something dawned on me. My thoughts returned to the Hukum Kanun Pahang, the manuscript I had spent so much time studying, and to the responsibilities of the Shahbandar within its account of government.
I began to see Tun Razak’s life through another lens: the tradition of service from which he came.
In an interview after the screening, I said, “It is in their blood, from one generation to another.”

I meant the understanding of responsibility that can grow within a family over generations. A child observes how his father serves, listens to the matters discussed around him and gradually learns what public office demands.

We understand this in a royal household. A prince learns something of the art of kingship by observing his father long before he is called upon to exercise it. Watching the documentary, I realised that a similar education took place in the household of a Shahbandar.
Tun Abdul Razak was himself the tenth Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar.
The Shahbandar had become Prime Minister.
There was something deeply moving in that thought. A son of Pahang had carried his upbringing, experience and understanding of duty into the service of an entire nation.

In Pahang, the Orang Besar Berempat comprises the Orang Kaya Indera Perba Jelai, Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar, Orang Kaya Indera Pahlawan and Orang Kaya Indera Segara. Each held responsibilities within the administration of the state, with a particular territory under his authority.

They supported the ruler in governing: offering counsel, administering affairs and exercising the authority entrusted to them. In modern terms, aspects of their work might be compared to the responsibilities of ministers. Their offices belonged, however, to a different political order, and were distinct from succession to the throne.
Of these four titles familiar to us in Pahang today, it was the Shahbandar that I encountered in my study of the Hukum Kanun Melaka and the Hukum Kanun Pahang.

That recognition returned to me during the screening. The Shahbandar was already an important officer in the world described by those legal texts. Centuries later, a man bearing that title would lead Malaysia.

The earlier office and the later hereditary Pahang title must be understood in their respective historical settings. Yet the connection invites us to look more closely at the traditions of government from which Tun Razak emerged.

There is an important distinction to make. The Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar holds office by royal appointment of the Sultan of Pahang. Although the title has remained within the same family across generations, it does not pass automatically from father to son.
Generations of Shahbandars have served Pahang’s rulers, offering counsel and assisting in the affairs of government according to the responsibilities of their time.
Across generations, this relationship has carried a continuing responsibility: to support the ruler in serving Pahang and its people.
Tun Razak was the tenth holder. His son, Najib, became the eleventh, and his grandson, Nizar, the twelfth.
The Sultan appoints the officeholder. The family can help prepare him to fulfil its responsibilities.
That preparation is what interests me.

A son growing up in such a household could observe how his father advised the ruler, received those seeking assistance and dealt with the affairs of the state. He could learn how to listen, how to weigh competing concerns and how to carry the expectations attached to the family’s position.
Just as a prince could learn the art of kingship from his father, a future Shahbandar could learn the responsibilities of government and service from him.

This is an inheritance that does not appear neatly in a family tree. Genealogy records names, relationships and the succession of titles. The knowledge passed through daily example is harder to trace, but deserves our attention.

The family’s history in Pahang reaches back to 1722 and to forebears who came from Sulawesi. That migration also carried knowledge and craftsmanship, including the weaving tradition associated with Tenun Pahang. The similarities between the textiles of Pahang and Sulawesi bear witness to a shared cultural history.

For me, this connection has particular meaning. My work with Tenun Pahang has taught me how knowledge survives through people: through hands that demonstrate, eyes that observe and younger generations willing to learn.
My study of the Hukum Kanun Pahang has brought me to another form of knowledge, the understanding of authority, duty and the ordering of a state.

At the screening, those two strands of my own work came together in an unexpected way. I found myself thinking about what families carry across generations, whether in craftsmanship or public service, and how that inheritance can find new expression.

Tun Razak succeeded his father as Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar in 1950. He became Pahang State Secretary in 1952 and Menteri Besar in 1955. His subsequent career took him to the offices of Deputy Prime Minister and Prime Minister of Malaysia.
His field of responsibility grew, from the affairs of Pahang to the affairs of a nation.

When I say that he carried Pahang to Malaysia, I mean that he brought something of his formation in Pahang into national service. His roots remained part of him as he undertook responsibilities far beyond the state from which he came.
Every appointment nevertheless demanded his own ability, judgment and commitment. An upbringing could prepare him; the work remained his to do.
That is why the documentary’s title is so fitting. Man Who Walked the Talk directs us to the actions through which he fulfilled his responsibilities.

Watching it, I saw both the man’s achievements and a question about his formation. What had he learned from the generations before him? What understanding of service had he absorbed in the household where he grew up? How might that experience have shaped the way he approached government?
These are questions worth exploring alongside the familiar record of his education and political career.

For me, the Hukum Kanun Pahang has made the offices of our earlier government more visible. Behind each title stood a person entrusted with responsibilities. Behind that person might stand generations of experience, remembered and taught within a family.
I had gone to watch a documentary about Tun Razak. I came away reflecting on the inheritance of an art: the art of governing, learned through example and proved through service.
The Shahbandar had become Prime Minister.
And a tradition of responsibility rooted in Pahang had found a larger field of service in Malaysia.
May Allah grant Tun Abdul Razak His mercy and reward him for the good he brought to the people.
Al-Fatihah.

Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia, and is currently a PhD candidate at ISTAC-IIUM.
19640f019f148359: Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington in September produced no major new agreement. But it did result in an extension of the trade truce that Xi and US president Donald Trump struck in Busan, South Korea, last October.
Instead of expiring on Nov 10, the truce will expire on Jan 10, 2027. Though modest, this achievement has given an unstable world economy a reprieve.

The core agreement is simple enough: China will refrain from enforcing the export controls on rare earths and related materials that it unveiled last October, and the US will refrain from raising tariffs further, holding the overall duty on Chinese goods near the 47% level reached in Busan (down from 57% beforehand).
Both sides have grumbled about compliance, but neither wants the truce to lapse before the presidents meet again, first in Shenzhen in November, then the following month in Miami.

China clearly has a great deal of leverage in dealing with Trump. It accounts for roughly 60–70% of global rare-earth mining and 85–90% of rare-earth processing (the step that turns mixed ores into the oxides used in many critical technologies).

And when it comes to the heavy rare-earth elements, China’s grip is even tighter. Processing of dysprosium and terbium, essential ingredients in electric-vehicle magnets, wind turbines, and missile-guidance systems, is carried out almost exclusively in China.

On a detailed element-by-element accounting, the US and its allies have meaningful non-Chinese extraction capacity for only seven or eight of the 17 rare earths, but essentially no processing capacity. That could change in the next two years, with the processing figure growing to five elements.

The Australian miner Lynas and the US-based MP Materials already ship commercial volumes of lighter elements like neodymium and praseodymium, and within ten years, non-Chinese extraction could cover nearly all light elements and most heavy ones.

But even then, the processing figure may reach only nine elements, with dysprosium and terbium remaining overwhelmingly under Chinese control. While future innovations in processing, or in designing rare earths out of manufactured goods altogether, could alter the picture, such scenarios are harder to predict.
It is also useful to question the belief that “de-risking” from China would leave the US and Europe unambiguously better off. Recent geopolitical developments suggest otherwise.
Now that the US no longer wants to be bound by international rules that it considers inconvenient, rare-earth leverage is one of the few remaining restraints on US protectionism and economic warfare.

Since the Trump administration seems oblivious to the cost of tariffs on US households, there is no guarantee that the next round of tariffs would stop at a level Americans can comfortably bear. In fact, by threatening to reduce, but not eliminate, the rare-earth supply, China may be saving Trump from himself, at least in the short term.
The European Union (EU) faces a similar situation. It has been more cautious than the US about raising tariffs on Chinese goods, partly because European industry is heavily reliant on Chinese inputs.
Although the EU’s own Critical Raw Materials Act targets 40% domestic processing by 2030, its auditors reported in February that actual capacity remains near 25%.

Tellingly, although Japan has spent over a decade and roughly US$1.2 billion diversifying away from China since a 2010 rare-earths dispute, its heavy rare-earth imports collapsed by 70–80% in early 2026.

Export controls were not invented by the Chinese. The US commerce department’s entity list has grown roughly ninefold over the past decade, to nearly 1,200 entries, while China’s own retaliatory lists have grown only through the occasional addition of a few dozen entities at a time. On this measure, the US and the EU currently maintain considerably longer control lists than China does.

Although export controls are nominally aimed at military applications, the national-security rationale is not always as clean as advertised, and the civilian collateral damage often rivals the intended effect.

In the case of the US and Chinese export controls, one unintended consequence has been a reduction in US exports and Chinese imports. This is probably because export controls cut off Chinese customers from US suppliers, who mostly failed to find replacement buyers and instead suffered a loss of revenue, profitability, and employment.

Whereas Oxford Economics estimates that export controls cost China a cumulative 0.8% of GDP in 2024–26, a 2023 input-output study concludes that the US has, in relative terms, lost more, with Japanese, South Korean, and European firms capturing the resulting market share.

In a world where the rules-based trading system is not functioning, a fragile status quo stabilised by mutual leverage is probably better than unilateral acts of dominance or chaos. If the zero-sum wrangling ultimately inspires a return to multilateral negotiation, so much the better.

Shang-Jin Wei, a former chief economist at the Asian Development Bank, is professor of finance and economics at Columbia Business School and Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.

Sehingga sekarang perang berterusan, dan Trump terus mengancam mahu menghapuskan Iran .

Selain pernah menjadi pesuruhjaya PBB mengenai hak asasi manusia, Navi Pillay juga pernah menjadi hakim Mahkamah Jenayah Antarabangsa dan pernah memegang jawatan presiden tribunal jenayah antarabangsa mengenai Rwanda dan sekarang memegang jawatan itu untuk tribunal mengenai Myanmar.

Saya tidak pasti sama ada kedudukan dan peranan Navi dalam Mahkamah Jenayah Antarabangsa atau ICC ada kena-mengena dengan tindakan pentadibran Trump mahu membubar atau “dismantle the ICC brick by brick,” kata Setiausaha Negara Marco Rubio.
Kata Rubio, AS akan mengenakan pelbagai sekatan termasuk cutting off the court’s resources to stop investigations into US personnel and allies like Israel.

Jelas AS tidak mahu ICC bertindak ke atas Tel Aviv meskipun Israel melakukan genosid di Gaza. Dan bagi AS, Mahkamah Jenayah Antarabangsa ‘tidak ada hak mengambil tindakan terhadap warganya’. Ertinya walaupun jika mereka melakukan jenayah antarabangsa.
Pada masa lalu ICC mengambil beberapa keputusan yang tidak disenangi AS dan Israel. ICC pernah keluarkan waran tangkap ke atas Netanyahu dan bekas menteri pertahanannya Yoav Gallant.

Setiausaha Agung PBB, Antonio Guterres menyifatkan keputusan pentadbiran Trump yang diumumkan pada hari Navi diisytihar pemenang Nobel Peace Prize 2026 a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice of which the ICC is a key pillar.
United Kingdom bersama Kanada, Denmark, Jerman, Perancis, Itali, Jepun dan Belanda menzahirkan rasa kesal terhadap tindakan AS dan strongly disagree with the sanctions.
Lapan negara itu menegaskan sokongan tidak berbelah bahagi dan berterusan terhadap ICC.
ICC adalah institusi kehakiman penting dalam membawa keadilan kepada mangsa jenayah antarabangsa. Sesungguhnya ia mesti dipertahankan. ‘Persetankan’ keputusan Trump.

f23750c0294ac548: In my previous column, I wrote about LIDAC26, the Luno Institutional Digital Asset Conference hosted by cryptocurrency exchange Luno in Kuala Lumpur on Sept 24, and confessed that my favourite session had nothing to do with regulators or stablecoins.
It was a breakout on Malaysian builders shaping the global digital asset landscape, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since.

Here's why. Talking to participants and reading reports, I found that if you have ever checked the price of a coin, traced a transaction on Ethereum or swapped one token for another on Solana (two of the world's busiest blockchains), there is a decent chance you used something that started in Malaysia, whether you knew it or not.

That's not just national pride talking: Tiger Research, a crypto research firm, said as much in its 2025 report on our market: "Etherscan, Jupiter, Virtuals Protocol, and CoinGecko all started in Malaysia and now have global reach."
The crypto world's price list

Start with CoinGecko, which Bobby Ong, an economics graduate of University College London, and TM Lee, who studied computer science at Purdue University, founded in Kuala Lumpur in April 2014. It began by tracking a mere 20 coins and now covers more than 21,000 crypto assets across over 1,000 exchanges, drawing what it says are more than 10 million users a month.
What I find most remarkable is how they got there, with no venture capital and no first hire until January 2018.

"Choosing not raising venture capital allowed us the opportunity to not need to relocate to Silicon Valley, one of the most expensive locations to live in," Ong told CryptoSlate in 2021, while Lee put it even more bluntly to The Edge: "There were no parents to bankroll us. We kept it low-cost and kept reinvesting; this helped us stay in the game."

In January, CoinDesk reported that CoinGecko was weighing a sale at a valuation of around RM2 billion. Not bad for a startup whose founders, The Edge reported in 2021, worked remotely before renting their first office in Taman Tun Dr Ismail.
The window into Ethereum
Then there is Etherscan, launched in 2015 by Matthew Tan. Think of it as a search engine for the Ethereum blockchain: punch in a wallet or transaction and it shows you exactly where the money went.

Back in 2019, The Edge reported that Tan was running the business out of Shah Alam with a team of just 15, and that it was already profitable. Since then, Etherscan says it has ranked among the world's top 1,000 websites by traffic, and in 2024 it bought Solscan, a popular explorer for the rival Solana blockchain.

Today, a team of more than 70 runs over 60 explorers, and developers can pull data from more than 50 blockchains with a single Etherscan key. That's right, the explorer Tan built and launched back in 2015 now reaches across much of the crypto world.
Solana's best-price finder

Next up is Jupiter, co-founded by Siong Ong, who sat on that LIDAC panel. Jupiter is an aggregator, which means it scans Solana's many trading venues for the best price and then makes the swap for you, even splitting your order across several venues if that gets you a better deal.

The numbers are staggering: according to data tracker DefiLlama, Jupiter has routed more than RM5 trillion in trades to date, and handled almost RM60 billion in the past 30 days alone, about half of all aggregator volume on Solana.
When Jupiter launched its JUP token in January 2024, it handed out a billion tokens to more than a million wallets, and it has since grown into perpetual futures, lending and a mobile wallet.
And the bench runs deep

Virtuals Protocol, co-founded by Jansen Teng, lets anyone launch and co-own artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Its token briefly topped a market value of RM20 billion in January 2025, and in February this year it launched Eastworld Labs to put humanoid robots to work, because, in Teng's words, they "are currently hamstrung by two fundamental bottlenecks: lack of data and capital".

Virtuals said more than 18,000 AI agents had already been deployed on its platform, alongside a fleet of more than 30 full-sized humanoid robots. Being in the robotics industry myself, I can tell you that is no small feat.

Then there is Pendle, a marketplace that lets investors trade the future yield on their crypto, a little like stripping a bond's coupons from its principal and selling them separately. Binance Labs, then the venture arm of the world's largest crypto exchange, backed it in 2023, and at its peak in September 2025 it held more than RM54 billion in deposits.
Tiger Research counts Pendle among the global projects in which "Malaysian talents also play key roles".

Sure, crypto is volatile, and several of these figures sit well below their peaks today. But the point is not the price of any single token; it is that a country of our size keeps producing the people who build tools much of the industry relies on.

Sitting in that breakout room two weeks ago, it struck me that the three founders on stage had, between them, built the price list, the search engine and the best-price finder that millions of crypto users lean on every day, and that all three companies started right here in Malaysia.
It's about time we celebrated them like the world-class builders they are.

86c42fc21c2ad724: From Khairul Hafezad Abdullah
When a heavy-rain warning appears on our phones, most of us understand what it means. We know which roads usually flood, which rivers may rise, and which neighbourhoods have been affected before.
Yet knowing that a risk exists is not the same as being prepared for it.

After a major flood, we often hear people say: “We never thought it would get this bad.” Often the problem is not always that we failed to see the danger. We saw it, understood it - and carried on as usual.

This is a familiar challenge in safety management. When people are repeatedly exposed to a hazard without serious consequences, their perception of risk can change. What once caused concern begins to feel normal.

Consider a family in a flood-prone area. The water may have reached the front gate several times but never entered the house. This past experience becomes reassurance: “It happens every year. The water will subside."
But the next flood does not have to behave like the last one. A hazard does not become less dangerous simply because we are accustomed to it.

Malaysia today has far better access to information than it did decades ago. Weather warnings reach our phones quickly, while river levels, road closures and evacuation centres can be monitored almost in real time.

The real question is what we do with that information. Do we move vehicles to higher ground, secure important documents and medicines, check on vulnerable family members or neighbours, and know where to go if evacuation becomes necessary? Or do we read the warning, glance outside, and continue as usual?

According to the statistics department, floods caused an estimated RM636.9 million in losses nationwide in 2025. Public assets and infrastructure accounted for RM380.2 million, while damage to living quarters amounted to RM183.8 million.
But preparedness should begin before we start counting losses.
Imagine being told you have 10 minutes to leave your house. What would you take? Who would need assistance? Where would you go? Would everyone know what to do?
For households with elderly people, young children, persons with disabilities or family members requiring regular medication, these questions matter even more.
Communities matter, too. In the first moments of an emergency, rescue personnel cannot be at every doorstep. Sometimes, the first person able to help is a neighbour.
A prepared community knows which households may need assistance, which roads become inaccessible first, and how reliable information can be shared quickly.

From an occupational safety viewpoint, good safety management does not wait for someone to be injured before action is taken. Hazards are identified, risks assessed and reasonable controls are introduced beforehand.
Why should disaster preparedness be any different?

Preparedness does not mean living in constant fear, nor does every warning require panic. It means accepting risk and uncertainty as part of the package, and taking reasonable action before circumstances become critical.
So when the next warning appears on our phones, perhaps the question should not be: “Will it really get that bad?” It should be: “If it does, are we ready to act?”
Khairul Hafezad Abdullah is a senior lecturer in occupational safety and health management, and a reader of FMT.

8d0d8c2963978094: The political backdrop was impossible to ignore as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim presented the 2027 budget.

With the next general elections (GE16) looming in a matter of months, most observers expected a flashier, election-winning plan aimed squarely at capturing votes highlighting the gains of Ekonomi Madani.
Instead, the 2027 budget arrived as a steady, work-a-day, “civil service” budget lacking a dramatic “wow factor”.

Choosing fiscal stability over electoral fireworks is a missed opportunity for a government seeking a renewed mandate but the reality is more nuanced. The complex political landscape of the unity government means a pragmatic, steady-as-she-goes approach was likely the only option Anwar had available.

On paper, the economic fundamentals driving the budget appear robust. Driven by strong macroeconomic growth of 5.7% in the first half of the year, record trade performance and rising investments including RM132 billion in the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, Anwar had room to manoeuvre.
Instead, the budget attempts to continue the dual ambition of “raising the ceiling” and “lifting the floor”.
The minimum wage rises to RM2,000, but only in eight months’ time. The higher RM2,500 benchmark for entry-level graduate positions will benefit a few but not many.

Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) was raised a little for its nine million core recipients and SARA-untuk-Semua was institutionalised with a tiny RM100 twice-yearly credit to the M40.

Meanwhile, civil servants on whom Anwar relies for what remains of his current term of office were given their share as usual. The general public on whom he relies for his next term of office were left wanting.
Higher personal income tax reliefs were finally announced but primarily benefit middle-to-higher income earners rather than lower-income households.
Notably absent was any reinstatement of the goods and services tax (GST), despite calls from business for structural tax reforms like indexed reliefs or alternative electronic payment taxes (EPTs).

Administrative fixes including resolving longstanding contract doctor issues with permanent appointments, launching the MediAsas coverage initiative help in the healthcare sector but there were no big reforms on elderly care.
Directing domestic investment through GLICs into sectors like semiconductors and AI infrastructure is a continuation of existing policies and not a new departure.

For everyday voters looking for immediate relief, the budget may feel underwhelming. The minimum wage increase, while positive, includes exemptions for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and the delayed implementation timeline leaves many low-wage workers feeling overlooked.
Meanwhile, fiscal consolidation metrics such as improved debt and deficit ratios are largely driven by higher GDP growth rather than structural spending cuts in borrowing.

In comparison to bolder shadow budgets and economic reform agendas which advocate for broad universal basic pensions, or expanded progressive wage schemes, this budget takes a conservative path. It held back from sweeping structural overhauls or aggressive handouts.
So, a big question is why did Anwar choose prudence over populism on the eve of an election? The answer lies in coalitional arithmetic.
Anwar leads a multi-coalition government where key partners hold significant leverage.

In the run-up to GE16, coalition allies are cautious about allowing the prime minister to deploy massive, popular pre-election handouts that could boost his popularity at their collective expense in contested seats.
Barisan Nasional does not want Anwar taking credit ahead of the election.
Consequently, the budget is a compromise. An administrative, predictable roadmap managed by fiscal conservatism.
It reassures markets and international investors while keeping the coalition intact.
It may not guarantee an electoral landslide but in the volatile arena of Malaysian politics, a steady hand on the wheel may well be the most realistic strategy Anwar could deploy.

d7c7b91ebc036608: Orang Melayu ada pepatah, sudah terhantuk baru tengadah. Maknanya, apabila sesuatu yang buruk berlaku, barulah kita sedar untuk berbuat sesuatu. Sesuatu yang dibuat itu sudah tentulah perubahan yang agak drastik supaya tidak terhantuk lagi. Namun demikian, dalam kes buli yang mengakibatkan kematian, kecederaan dan trauma, orang Melayu seperti ‘sudah terhantuk terus lali dan tidur’. Sebabnya, banyak insiden yang terpaksa kita tanggung sebagai rakyat dan orang Melayu, tetapi ia tetap berlaku. Selang beberapa hari di Negeri Sembilan yang kini tersohor dengan kemelut pemerintahan tidak berkesudahan, kita dengar kes buli di sekolah berasrama. Ada juga kes buli yang mengakibatkan kematian di sekolah awam, tetapi perkara itu, bagi saya lebih mudah diselesaikan. Saya hendak cuba selesaikan masalah buli di sekolah berasrama dulu sebab ia paling teruk dan memalukan orang Melayu. Sebabnya kita tak pernah dengar kes buli yang mencederakan mangsa, mati atau trauma dari sekolah vernakular Cina atau India. Mungkin sebab sekolah vernakular tidak ada asrama penuh seperti orang Melayu.

Saya mendesak semua sekolah berasrama ditutup, paling kurang enam bulan atau setahun. Sudah tentu akan ada backlash besar daripada ibu bapa yang lebih mementingkan pelajaran. Cadangan saya adalah semua pelajar sekolah berasrama ditempatkan sementara di sekolah awam berdekatan sehingga segala peralatan keselamatan, SOP pentadbiran dan latihan mengenal pasti buli yang disertai semua guru sekolah agama dilaksanakan.

Pertamanya, Kementerian Pendidikan dan Majlis Amanah Rakyat (Mara) perlu membiayai audit di semua sekolah berasrama yang akan dijalankan sebuah firma audit keselamatan paling profesional. Mungkin firma ini mempunyai kriteria audit sendiri, tetapi saya ingin mengemukakan beberapa pemerhatian saya untuk diambil kira.

Pertama, audit perlu dijalankan terhadap keberkesanan penempatan CCTV di tempat strategik, bukan ikut suka pentadbir sekolah. Jumlah dan visual coverage CCTV perlu ditentukan secara khusus dan mengikut kajian mendalam, selain mewujudkan bilik kawalan CCTV oleh pengawal terlatih.

Kedua, cadangan saya bahawa pengasingan asrama untuk pelajar senior dan junior perlu dilakukan supaya tidak bercampur di luar bilik darjah. Tempat sembahyang, kantin, riadah dan tandas perlu diasingkan atau mengikut giliran supaya tiada percampuran senior dan junior langsung. Audit harus memastikan perkara paling penting ini.

Ketiga, cadangan saya supaya warden dan pengawal keselamatan meronda sekeliling sekolah dan asrama secara rambang sekurang-kurangnya tiga kali setiap hari, walaupun CCTV beroperasi. Imej pengawal meronda penting supaya pembuli tidak berani bertindak sewenang-wenangnya. Penggunaan dron sebagai kawalan tambahan boleh dijadikan amalan keselamatan.

Keempat, audit harus memastikan semua pintu bilik darjah, dewan atau makmal dan setor dikunci apabila tidak digunakan. Kematian pelajar Tingkatan 4, Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairoul Faisal di sebuah sekolah di Yong Peng, Johor mungkin dapat dihalang, jika pintu dewan dikunci, tetapi kini 'nasi sudah menjadi bubur'.

Kelima, semua guru sekolah harus mengikuti kursus mengenal pasti buli dalam kalangan pelajar serta membuat persediaan seperti kaedah menyoal pelajar, pemerhatian kelas serta penulisan laporan tindakan kepada guru disiplin. Guru yang sekolah asrama diaudit akan ditempatkan di sekolah berdekatan rumah mereka selepas kursus disempurnakan.

Keenam, audit juga perlu memastikan 'penalti' dikenakan terhadap kakitangan pentadbiran dan warden apabila kejadian buli mengakibatkan kecederaan serius serta kematian. Setakat ini, tidak kira berapa ramai pelajar yang mati atau cedera dibuli, kakitangan pentadbiran tetap dinaikkan pangkat dan gaji bertambah setiap tahun.

Akhir sekali, tiba masanya menyimpulkan kebenaran yang perit, penyeliaan sekolah berasrama gagal menjadi payung keselamatan dan kesihatan anak Melayu kita. Kita perlu menyifatkan masalah buli sebagai threat to nation dan mencari kaedah terbaik untuk menyelesaikannya.
